questions.stem: A block of mass $m = 5\text{ kg}$ is pulled along a smooth horizontal surface by a constant pulling force $F = 40\text{ N}$ directed at an angle $\theta = 60^\circ$ above the horizontal. If the block is displaced horizontally by $d = 10\text{ m}$, what is the total work done by the pulling force?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Projecting the pulling force along the horizontal displacement using W = F * d * cos(60°) = 40 * 10 * 0.5 = 200 J.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires vector projection onto the displacement axis rather than unprojected scalar recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: W = F * d * cos(theta) = 40 * 10 * cos(60°) = 400 * 0.5 = 200 J.

B.diagnostic: Omitted cosine factor: multiplied scalar magnitudes directly W = F * d = 40 * 10 = 400 J.

C.diagnostic: Used vertical sine component: W = F * d * sin(60°) = 400 * (sqrt(3)/2) = 200*sqrt(3) J.

D.diagnostic: Assumed force was completely perpendicular to displacement yielding zero work.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the physical definition of mechanical work done by a constant force vector?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Work is the scalar dot product of the force vector and the displacement vector: $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = F d \cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Component Projection
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Which component of the pulling force contributes to the horizontal displacement?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Only the component parallel to the displacement contributes to work: $F_{\parallel} = F\cos 60^\circ = 40 \times 0.5 = 20\text{ N}$. The perpendicular vertical component ($F\sin 60^\circ$) does zero work because there is no vertical displacement.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the product of the parallel force component and the $10\text{ m}$ displacement?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $W = F_{\parallel} \times d = (20\text{ N}) \times (10\text{ m}) = 200\text{ J}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Block of mass $5\text{ kg}$ pulled by $40\text{ N}$ at $60^\circ$ above horizontal over $d = 10\text{ m}$. Goal: find work done by pulling force.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Cartesian coordinate system: $+x$ along horizontal surface, $+y$ upward. $\vec{F} = 40\cos(60^\circ)\hat{i} + 40\sin(60^\circ)\hat{j} = 20\hat{i} + 20\sqrt{3}\hat{j}\text{ N}$. Displacement $\vec{d} = 10\hat{i}\text{ m}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Definition of mechanical work: $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = F_x d_x + F_y d_y$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $W = (20\text{ N})(10\text{ m}) + (20\sqrt{3}\text{ N})(0\text{ m}) = 200\text{ J}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Half of the applied force magnitude ($20\text{ N}$) accelerates the block forward doing $200\text{ J}$ of work; the other half lifts upward against gravity without doing work because vertical displacement is zero.

derivation_steps: Definition of work: $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = F d \cos\theta$.
Given values: $F = 40\text{ N}, d = 10\text{ m}, \theta = 60^\circ$.
Evaluate cosine: $\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$.
Compute scalar product: $W = (40\text{ N})(10\text{ m})(0.5) = 200\text{ J}$.

limiting_cases.expected: cos(90°) = 0 => W = 0 J (Zero work along horizontal)

independent_check.quick_check: Ratio $W / (F d) = 200 / 400 = 0.5 = \cos 60^\circ$. Exactly verified.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Work-Energy Theorem: If starting from rest, acceleration $a = F_x / m = 20 / 5 = 4\text{ m/s}^2$. Velocity after $10\text{ m}$: $v^2 = 2 a d = 2(4)(10) = 80\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$. Kinetic energy: $K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{1}{2}(5)(80) = 200\text{ J}$. Matches $W = 200\text{ J}$ with zero residual.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT multiply force by displacement without the cosine factor; work depends strictly on the component along the displacement.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-01 (Definition of Mechanical Work)

questions.stem: A satellite of mass $m$ orbits the Earth in a uniform circular orbit of radius $R$ with constant orbital speed $v_0$. What is the net work done on the satellite by the gravitational force during one complete orbit of period $T$?

system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial geocentric frame with origin at Earth center

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Explaining that the centripetal gravitational force is everywhere perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity vector (cos 90° = 0), yielding zero differential work dW = 0 throughout.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires physical justification of the perpendicular invariant F perp v, not bare recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: At every instant, the gravitational force acts radially inward while velocity is strictly tangential (F perp v => cos 90° = 0). Thus dW = F . dr = 0 at every point, giving total work W = 0 J.

B.diagnostic: Confused work done with gravitational potential energy magnitude G*M*m/R.

C.diagnostic: Multiplied gravitational force by orbit circumference 2*pi*R, ignoring that force is perpendicular to path.

D.diagnostic: Equated work to satellite kinetic energy 1/2 m v_0^2.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the angle between the gravitational force vector and the satellite's instantaneous velocity vector in a circular orbit?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: In a circular orbit, gravity points radially inward toward the Earth's center, while the velocity vector is directed along the circle tangent. The angle between radius and tangent is identically $90^\circ$ ($ec{F}_g \perp \vec{v}$).

progressive_hints.title: Differential Work Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the differential work $dW = \vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{r}$ done during an infinitesimal displacement along the orbit?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $dW = \vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{r} = F_g ds \cos 90^\circ = 0$. Since work is zero at every infinitesimal instant of the flight, the integral over any portion (or full orbit) is identically zero.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What does the Work-Energy Theorem predict about the change in the satellite's kinetic energy over a circular orbit?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$. Since orbital speed $v_0$ is constant in uniform circular motion, $\Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv_0^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_0^2 = 0$. Therefore, the net work must be exactly $0\text{ J}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Satellite of mass $m$ in uniform circular orbit of radius $R$ at speed $v_0$. Goal: find work done by gravity over one complete revolution.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$. Gravitational force: $\vec{F}_g = -\frac{G M m}{R^2}\hat{r}$. Displacement element along circular path: $d\vec{r} = R d\theta\hat{\theta}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Work integral: $W = \oint \vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{r}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $\vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{r} = \left(-\frac{G M m}{R^2}\hat{r}\right) \cdot (R d\theta\hat{\theta}) = 0$ because $\hat{r} \cdot \hat{\theta} = 0$. Thus $W = \int_0^{2\pi} 0 = 0\text{ J}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: A perpendicular force changes the direction of motion without altering speed; it neither adds nor removes kinetic energy from the orbiting body.

derivation_steps: Gravitational force is purely radial: $\vec{F}_g = -F_g\hat{r}$.
Displacement in circular orbit is purely azimuthal: $d\vec{r} = R d\theta\hat{\theta}$.
Evaluate scalar product: $\vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{r} = -F_g R (\hat{r} \cdot \hat{\theta}) d\theta = 0$.
Integrate around orbit: $W = \oint dW = \int_0^{2\pi} 0 = 0\text{ J}$.

limiting_cases.expected: oint F_c . dr = 0 J identically for any conservative field

independent_check.quick_check: Kinetic energy is constant at $K = \frac{1}{2}mv_0^2$. $\Delta K = 0 \implies W_{\text{net}} = 0\text{ J}$. Verified.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Gravity is a conservative force: $\oint \vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{r} = 0$ for ANY closed path, whether circular or elliptical. Because the orbit begins and ends at the exact same point in space, $W = -\Delta U = 0\text{ J}$.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT confuse the non-zero centripetal acceleration ($a_c = v_0^2/R$) with non-zero work; acceleration can be non-zero while work is identically zero.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-01 (Definition of Mechanical Work)

questions.stem: Two bodies $A$ and $B$ have masses $m_A = 2\text{ kg}$ and $m_B = 8\text{ kg}$ respectively. If both bodies have the exact same linear momentum magnitude $p$, what is the ratio of their kinetic energies $\frac{K_A}{K_B}$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two uncoupled moving particles A and B

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying K = p^2 / (2m) to deduce inverse mass proportionality: K_A / K_B = m_B / m_A = 8 / 2 = 4.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires algebraic scaling transformation between momentum and kinetic energy.

A.diagnostic: Correct: K = p^2 / (2m). Since p is identical, K is inversely proportional to m: K_A / K_B = m_B / m_A = 8 / 2 = 4 : 1.

B.diagnostic: Assumed kinetic energy is directly proportional to mass: K_A / K_B = m_A / m_B = 2 / 8 = 1 : 4 (valid only for equal speeds, not equal momentum).

C.diagnostic: Assumed equal momentum implies equal kinetic energy: 1 : 1.

D.diagnostic: Squared the mass ratio: (8/2)^2 = 16 : 1.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the relationship expressing kinetic energy $K$ directly in terms of momentum $p$ and mass $m$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Since momentum is $p = m v \implies v = \frac{p}{m}$, substituting into kinetic energy yields: $K = \frac{1}{2}m v^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\left(\frac{p}{m}\right)^2 = \frac{p^2}{2m}$.

progressive_hints.title: Inverse Scaling Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: When two objects have identical momentum $p$, how does kinetic energy scale with mass?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Because $p$ is constant, $K \propto \frac{1}{m}$. Therefore, the ratio of kinetic energies is inversely proportional to the ratio of their masses: $\frac{K_A}{K_B} = \frac{m_B}{m_A}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the numerical evaluation of $\frac{m_B}{m_A}$ for $m_B = 8\text{ kg}$ and $m_A = 2\text{ kg}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\frac{K_A}{K_B} = \frac{8\text{ kg}}{2\text{ kg}} = 4$. Thus, the ratio is $4 : 1$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Bodies $A$ and $B$ have masses $m_A = 2\text{ kg}, m_B = 8\text{ kg}$ and equal momentum $p$. Goal: evaluate ratio $K_A / K_B$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Kinetic energy relation: $K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$. Let $p_A = p_B = p$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: $K_A = \frac{p^2}{2m_A}$ and $K_B = \frac{p^2}{2m_B}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Divide: $\frac{K_A}{K_B} = \frac{p^2/(2m_A)}{p^2/(2m_B)} = \frac{m_B}{m_A} = \frac{8}{2} = 4$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: For a fixed momentum, the lighter particle moves four times faster ($v_A = 4 v_B$), and because kinetic energy depends quadratically on speed, it carries four times more kinetic energy.

derivation_steps: Definition of momentum: $p = m v$.
Express velocity: $v = p / m$.
Substitute into kinetic energy: $K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{1}{2} m (p/m)^2 = \frac{p^2}{2m}$.
Apply to bodies $A$ and $B$: $K_A = \frac{p^2}{2m_A}$, $K_B = \frac{p^2}{2m_B}$.
Form ratio: $\frac{K_A}{K_B} = \frac{m_B}{m_A} = \frac{8\text{ kg}}{2\text{ kg}} = 4 : 1$.

independent_check.quick_check: Choose test momentum $p = 8\text{ kg m/s}$. Speed $v_A = p / m_A = 8 / 2 = 4\text{ m/s}$. Speed $v_B = p / m_B = 8 / 8 = 1\text{ m/s}$. $K_A = \frac{1}{2}(2)(4^2) = 16\text{ J}$. $K_B = \frac{1}{2}(8)(1^2) = 4\text{ J}$. Ratio $K_A / K_B = 16 / 4 = 4$. Exact match.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Gun and bullet recoil analogy: Gun and bullet have equal and opposite momentum $p$. The ratio of bullet energy to gun energy is $m_{\text{gun}} / m_{\text{bullet}} \gg 1$, proving lighter mass carries vastly higher kinetic energy. Physical principle verified.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT use $K \propto m$; that is only true if speeds are equal. When momenta are equal, $K \propto 1/m$.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-10 (Momentum vs Kinetic Energy Scaling)

questions.stem: An electric water pump lifts $1200\text{ kg}$ of water from a well of depth $h = 15\text{ m}$ in a time of $t = 60\text{ s}$ at constant speed. What is the average power output of the pump? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

idealizations: Constant elevation speed (zero net kinetic energy change)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating gravitational potential energy gain W = mgh = 180,000 J and computing rate of delivery P = W / t = 180,000 / 60 = 3000 W.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires work-power conversion and unit rate reduction.

B.diagnostic: Reported total work done in Joules (180,000 J) as power in Watts, neglecting time division by 60 s.

C.diagnostic: Omitted depth h: computed (1200 * 10) / 60 = 1200 W.

D.diagnostic: Divided mass directly by depth and time: 1200 / (15 * 60) or similar crude miscalculation.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the total mechanical work required to lift a mass $m$ to a height $h$ against gravity?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The work required to lift mass $m$ at constant speed against gravity is equal to the increase in gravitational potential energy: $W = m g h$.

progressive_hints.title: Work Evaluation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the numerical work for $m = 1200\text{ kg}, g = 10\text{ m/s}^2,$ and $h = 15\text{ m}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $W = 1200\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m/s}^2 \times 15\text{ m} = 180{,}000\text{ J}$ ($180\text{ kJ}$).

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How is power defined from work and elapsed time, and what is the output in Watts?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Power is the rate of doing work: $P = \frac{W}{t}$. For $W = 180{,}000\text{ J}$ and $t = 60\text{ s}$: $P = \frac{180{,}000}{60} = 3000\text{ W}$ ($3\text{ kW}$).

reasoning_ladder.understand: Pump lifts $1200\text{ kg}$ of water through $h = 15\text{ m}$ in $t = 60\text{ s}$ at constant speed. Goal: calculate average power output.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Vertical coordinate axis with origin at well bottom. Water lifted from $y = 0$ to $y = 15\text{ m}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Work: $W = \Delta U = mgh$. Power: $P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{mgh}{t}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The pump delivers energy at the rate of $3000\text{ Joules per second}$ ($3\text{ kW}$), which is roughly equivalent to a $4\text{ horsepower}$ electric motor.

derivation_steps: Work done to lift water: $W = mgh$.
Substitute values: $W = 1200\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m/s}^2 \times 15\text{ m} = 180{,}000\text{ J}$.
Definition of power: $P = \frac{W}{t}$.
Divide by elapsed time: $P = \frac{180{,}000\text{ J}}{60\text{ s}} = 3000\text{ W} = 3\text{ kW}$.

independent_check.quick_check: Mass flow rate: $\frac{dm}{dt} = \frac{1200\text{ kg}}{60\text{ s}} = 20\text{ kg/s}$. Power formula: $P = \left(\frac{dm}{dt}\right) g h = 20 \times 10 \times 15 = 3000\text{ W}$. Exact match.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Average vertical lifting speed: $v = \frac{h}{t} = \frac{15\text{ m}}{60\text{ s}} = 0.25\text{ m/s}$. Average upward force required: $F = mg = 1200 \times 10 = 12{,}000\text{ N}$. Power: $P = F v = 12{,}000 \times 0.25 = 3000\text{ W}$. Exactly verified.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT report Joules when asked for Watts; Joules measures total work, while Watts measures the rate of energy transfer.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-08 (Power as Rate of Energy Transfer)

questions.topic: Work, Energy & Power: Conservative Fields & Potential Wells
questions.stem: A body moves along the $+x$-axis under the action of a variable force $F(x)$ shown in the accompanying graph (Figure WEP-05). The force increases linearly from $0$ to $20\text{ N}$ between $x = 0$ and $x = 4\text{ m}$, and then remains constant at $20\text{ N}$ from $x = 4\text{ m}$ to $x = 8\text{ m}$. What is the total work done by the force as the body moves from $x = 0$ to $x = 8\text{ m}$?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating the work as the area under the F-x graph partitioned into a triangle (1/2 * 4 * 20 = 40 J) plus a rectangle (4 * 20 = 80 J) to get 120 J.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires geometric partitioning and graphical representation synthesis.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Area under F-x curve = Area of triangle [0 to 4 m] + Area of rectangle [4 to 8 m] = (1/2 * 4 * 20) + (4 * 20) = 40 + 80 = 120 J.

B.diagnostic: Treated the entire 8 m as a constant 20 N force: 8 * 20 = 160 J.

C.diagnostic: Only computed the work in the constant force region: 4 * 20 = 80 J, omitting the initial triangular ramp.

D.diagnostic: Only computed the work in the triangular ramp region: 1/2 * 4 * 20 = 40 J.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What geometric feature of a force-displacement graph represents mechanical work?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By the definition of work for a variable force, $W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) dx$. This definite integral corresponds precisely to the area under the $F-x$ curve bounded by the displacement axis.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Partitioning Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Into what standard geometric shapes can the area under $F(x)$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 8\text{ m}$ be partitioned?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The region splits into two sections: 1) A right triangle from $x = 0$ to $x = 4\text{ m}$ with base $4\text{ m}$ and height $20\text{ N}$. 2) A rectangle from $x = 4$ to $x = 8\text{ m}$ with base $4\text{ m}$ and height $20\text{ N}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the sum of the areas of the triangle and the rectangle?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Triangle area: $\frac{1}{2} \times 4\text{ m} \times 20\text{ N} = 40\text{ J}$. Rectangle area: $4\text{ m} \times 20\text{ N} = 80\text{ J}$. Total work: $W = 40 + 80 = 120\text{ J}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Force $F(x)$ increases linearly from $0$ to $20\text{ N}$ over $x \in [0, 4]$, then constant $20\text{ N}$ over $x \in [4, 8]$. Goal: find total work from $x = 0$ to $8\text{ m}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Force function: $F(x) = 5x$ for $x \in [0, 4]$, and $F(x) = 20$ for $x \in [4, 8]$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Work is the definite integral: $W = \int_0^8 F(x) dx = \int_0^4 5x dx + \int_4^8 20 dx$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The total work of $120\text{ J}$ matches the area of a trapezoid with parallel sides $b_1 = 8\text{ m}$ and $b_2 = 4\text{ m}$ and height $h = 20\text{ N}$.

derivation_steps: Definition of work: $W = \int_0^8 F(x) dx$.
Split integral across piecewise intervals: $W = \int_0^4 F(x) dx + \int_4^8 F(x) dx$.
Area 1 (Triangle): $A_1 = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4\text{ m} \times 20\text{ N} = 40\text{ J}$.
Area 2 (Rectangle): $A_2 = \text{base} \times \text{height} = (8 - 4)\text{ m} \times 20\text{ N} = 80\text{ J}$.
Total work: $W = A_1 + A_2 = 40\text{ J} + 80\text{ J} = 120\text{ J}$.

independent_check.quick_check: Trapezoid formula: Area $= \frac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2) h = \frac{1}{2}(8 + 4) \times 20 = 6 \times 20 = 120\text{ J}$. Exact one-line verification.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Average force method: In phase 1, average force is $\frac{0 + 20}{2} = 10\text{ N}$; work $= 10 \times 4 = 40\text{ J}$. In phase 2, average force is $20\text{ N}$; work $= 20 \times 4 = 80\text{ J}$. Total $W = 40 + 80 = 120\text{ J}$. Validated.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT multiply the peak force by the full displacement ($20 \times 8 = 160\text{ J}$); the force starts at zero and only reaches $20\text{ N}$ after $4\text{ m}$.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-02 (Work by Variable Forces & Spring Integration)

questions.stem: An ideal horizontal spring with spring constant $k = 400\text{ N/m}$ is fixed to a rigid wall. A block of mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ is pushed against the spring, compressing it by $x = 0.1\text{ m}$ from its natural equilibrium length. When released from rest on a frictionless horizontal floor, what is the speed of the block as it passes through the equilibrium position ($x = 0$)?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Equating stored elastic potential energy U = 1/2 k x^2 to final kinetic energy K = 1/2 m v^2 to find v = x * sqrt(k/m) = 0.1 * sqrt(200) = sqrt(2) m/s.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires conservation of mechanical energy balance between spring well and kinetic state.

B.diagnostic: Spring work fallacy: used k x^2 = 1/2 m v^2 (forgetting 1/2 in spring potential) yielding v = 2.0 m/s.

C.diagnostic: Included an extra factor of 2 in the denominator yielding v = 1.0 m/s.

D.diagnostic: Forgot square root on v^2 yielding 4.0 m/s or miscalculated sqrt(200).

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What conservation law governs the release of a spring-block system on a frictionless surface?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Because the floor is frictionless and the spring force is conservative, total mechanical energy is conserved: $E = U_s + K = \text{constant}$.

progressive_hints.title: Energy Balance Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the algebraic expression equating initial potential energy to kinetic energy at equilibrium?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: At maximum compression: $K_i = 0$, $U_i = \frac{1}{2} k x^2$. At equilibrium ($x = 0$): $U_f = 0$, $K_f = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$. Therefore: $\frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \implies v = x\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the speed for $k = 400\text{ N/m}, m = 2\text{ kg},$ and $x = 0.1\text{ m}$?

reasoning_ladder.understand: Spring of $k = 400\text{ N/m}$ compressed by $0.1\text{ m}$ releases mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ on smooth floor. Goal: find speed at $x = 0$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Energy states: Initial state (compressed): $x_1 = 0.1\text{ m}, v_1 = 0$. Final state (equilibrium): $x_2 = 0, v_2 = v$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Mechanical energy conservation: $\Delta K + \Delta U = 0 \implies \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - 0 = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 - 0$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $\frac{1}{2}(2)v^2 = \frac{1}{2}(400)(0.1)^2 \implies v^2 = 200(0.01) = 2 \implies v = \sqrt{2}\text{ m/s} \approx 1.41\text{ m/s}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: All $2\text{ Joules}$ of stored elastic potential energy in the compressed spring converts completely into kinetic energy of the block.

derivation_steps: Elastic potential energy in compressed spring: $U = \frac{1}{2} k x^2$.
Substitute values: $U = \frac{1}{2}(400\text{ N/m})(0.1\text{ m})^2 = 200 \times 0.01 = 2\text{ J}$.
By conservation of mechanical energy, this equals kinetic energy at equilibrium: $K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = 2\text{ J}$.
Solve for speed: $\frac{1}{2}(2\text{ kg}) v^2 = 2\text{ J} \implies v^2 = 2 \implies v = \sqrt{2}\text{ m/s} \approx 1.41\text{ m/s}$.

independent_check.quick_check: From SHM dynamics: $v_{\max} = \omega A$. Angular frequency $\omega = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{400/2} = \sqrt{200} = 10\sqrt{2}\text{ rad/s}$. Amplitude $A = 0.1\text{ m}$. Speed: $v = (10\sqrt{2})(0.1) = \sqrt{2}\text{ m/s}$. Exact match.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Average acceleration check: Maximum force $F_{\max} = kx = 400(0.1) = 40\text{ N}$. Average acceleration $\bar{a} \approx 10\text{ m/s}^2$. Time to quarter cycle $t = \frac{\pi}{2\omega} = \frac{\pi}{20\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.111\text{ s}$. $v \approx \bar{a} t \approx 1.4\text{ m/s}$. Consistent.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT assume $U = k x^2$; the factor of $1/2$ comes from the triangular area of the linear Hooke's law force $F(x') = k x'$.

questions.stem: A car of mass $m$ traveling at speed $v$ skids to a complete stop over a braking distance $s_1$ on a horizontal asphalt road when the driver locks the wheels. If the initial speed is doubled to $2v$ under identical road and tire friction conditions, what will be the new skid distance $s_2$?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling braking distance through Work-Energy Theorem: f_k * s = 1/2 m v^2 => s is proportional to v^2, so doubling v quadruples the skid distance.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires quadratic scaling modeling of kinetic energy dissipation against non-conservative friction.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Work-energy theorem: -f_k * s = 0 - 1/2 m v^2 => s = m v^2 / (2 f_k). Since f_k is constant, s is proportional to v^2. Doubling speed yields (2)^2 s_1 = 4 s_1.

B.diagnostic: Assumed stopping distance scales linearly with speed: s_2 = 2 s_1 (confusing stopping distance with stopping time Delta t = m v / f_k).

C.diagnostic: Applied square root scaling: s_2 = sqrt(2) s_1.

D.diagnostic: Assumed cubic scaling: s_2 = 2^3 s_1 = 8 s_1.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What connects the initial kinetic energy of the car to the work done by the braking friction force?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By the Work-Energy Theorem, the work done by the retarding friction force equals the change in kinetic energy: $W_{\text{friction}} = \Delta K \implies -f_k s = 0 - \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Proportionality Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How does the stopping distance $s$ depend mathematically on the initial speed $v$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Solving for distance: $s = \frac{m v^2}{2 f_k} = \frac{v^2}{2 \mu_k g}$. Because mass $m$ and friction force $f_k$ are unchanged, the stopping distance is directly proportional to the SQUARE of the speed: $s \propto v^2$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: If initial speed $v$ is replaced by $2v$, by what factor does $s$ multiply?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $s_2 \propto (2v)^2 = 4v^2 = 4 s_1$. Thus, the new stopping distance is $4 s_1$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Car traveling at $v$ stops over distance $s_1$. Condition: speed doubles to $2v$ under same friction. Goal: find new distance $s_2$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Forces on car during skid: normal force $N = mg$, kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k mg$ opposing motion.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Work-Energy Theorem: $W_{\text{net}} = K_f - K_i \implies -f_k s = 0 - \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \implies s = \frac{mv^2}{2f_k}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Case 1: $s_1 = \frac{m v^2}{2f_k}$. Case 2: $s_2 = \frac{m (2v)^2}{2f_k} = \frac{4 m v^2}{2f_k} = 4 s_1$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Doubling vehicular speed does not merely double the braking distance; it quadruples it, because kinetic energy grows with the square of speed.

derivation_steps: Work-Energy theorem: $W_{\text{fric}} = \Delta K$.
Work done by kinetic friction: $W_{\text{fric}} = -f_k s$.
Change in kinetic energy: $\Delta K = 0 - \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = -\frac{1}{2} m v^2$.
Equate: $-f_k s = -\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \implies s = \frac{m v^2}{2 f_k}$.
Substitute $v \to 2v$: $s_2 = \frac{m (2v)^2}{2 f_k} = 4\left(\frac{m v^2}{2 f_k}\right) = 4 s_1$.

independent_check.quick_check: From kinematics: $v_f^2 = v_i^2 - 2 a s \implies 0 = v^2 - 2 a s \implies s = \frac{v^2}{2a}$. With constant deceleration $a = \mu_k g$, $s \propto v^2$. Doubling $v$ quadruples $s$. Exactly verified.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Stopping time: $v = a t \implies t = v/a$. Stopping distance is average speed times time: $s = \bar{v} t = \left(\frac{v}{2}\right)\left(\frac{v}{a}\right) = \frac{v^2}{2a}$. Both time and average speed double, so their product quadruples: $2 \times 2 = 4$.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT confuse stopping distance ($s \propto v^2$) with stopping time ($t \propto v$); while stopping time only doubles, the car travels four times as far.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-03 (Work-Energy Theorem)

questions.stem: A particle moves in 1D along the $x$-axis subject to a conservative force corresponding to potential energy function $U(x) = 5 x^2 - 20 x + 15$, where $x$ is in meters and $U$ is in Joules. What is the value of the force $F(x)$ acting on the particle at position $x = 3\text{ m}$?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Differentiating U(x) and applying the negative sign F(x) = -dU/dx = -(10x - 20) = -10x + 20, evaluating at x = 3 m to get -10 N.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires derivative calculus evaluation and negative sign preservation.

B.diagnostic: Forgot the defining negative sign: computed +dU/dx = 10(3) - 20 = +10 N.

C.diagnostic: Assumed force is zero at x = 3 m (confusing it with the equilibrium point at x = 2 m where dU/dx = 0).

D.diagnostic: Omitted the +20 term and computed -10(3) = -30 N.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the mathematical relation between a conservative force and its potential energy function in 1D?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: A conservative force is the NEGATIVE spatial derivative (negative gradient) of the potential energy: $F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx}$.

progressive_hints.title: Differentiation Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the derivative $\frac{dU}{dx}$ for $U(x) = 5x^2 - 20x + 15$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Using power rule: $\frac{dU}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx}(5x^2 - 20x + 15) = 10x - 20$. Therefore, the force function is $F(x) = -\left(\frac{dU}{dx}\right) = -(10x - 20) = -10x + 20$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the value of $F(x)$ at $x = 3\text{ m}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $F(3) = -10(3) + 20 = -30 + 20 = -10\text{ N}$ (directed in the negative x-direction, restoring the particle toward equilibrium at $x=2$).

reasoning_ladder.understand: Potential energy function $U(x) = 5x^2 - 20x + 15$. Goal: find force $F$ at position $x = 3\text{ m}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: 1D potential curve $U(x)$. Conservative force relation: $F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Differentiate $U(x)$ with respect to $x$ and apply the negative sign.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The potential minimum (equilibrium) is at $x = 2\text{ m}$. At $x = 3\text{ m}$, the particle is displaced to the right, experiencing a restoring force of $10\text{ N}$ directed to the left (negative x).

derivation_steps: Fundamental conservative force relation: $F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx}$.
Differentiate: $\frac{dU}{dx} = 10 x - 20$.
Apply negative sign: $F(x) = -(10 x - 20) = -10 x + 20$.

limiting_cases.expected: F = -10(1) + 20 = +10 N (Restoring force points right toward equilibrium)

independent_check.quick_check: Complete the square: $U(x) = 5(x^2 - 4x + 4) - 20 + 15 = 5(x-2)^2 - 5$. This is a harmonic oscillator potential with effective spring constant $k = 10\text{ N/m}$ centered at $x_0 = 2\text{ m}$. Restoring force: $F = -k(x - x_0) = -10(3 - 2) = -10(1) = -10\text{ N}$. Exactly matches.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT forget the negative sign in $F = -dU/dx$; particles are pushed DOWN the potential hill toward lower potential energy, not up it.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-06 (Conservative Force as Negative Potential Gradient)

questions.stem: An elevator cab of total mass $M = 1000\text{ kg}$ is hoisted upward by a motorized steel cable. Starting from rest, the elevator accelerates uniformly upward at $a = 2\text{ m/s}^2$ for the first $4\text{ s}$. What is the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by the tension force in the cable at time $t = 3\text{ s}$? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Elevator cab under vertical cable tension
idealizations: Negligible cable mass and pulley friction

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating dynamic cable tension T = M(g + a) = 12,000 N, kinematic speed v(3) = a * t = 6 m/s, and instantaneous power P = T * v = 72,000 W = 72 kW.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires combining Newton II dynamic tension with kinematic speed and instantaneous power product.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Tension T = M(g + a) = 1000(10 + 2) = 12,000 N. Speed at t = 3 s: v = a * t = 2 * 3 = 6 m/s. Instantaneous power P = T * v = 12,000 * 6 = 72,000 W = 72 kW.

B.diagnostic: Used static weight T = Mg = 10,000 N: P = 10,000 * 6 = 60 kW, neglecting upward acceleration force.

C.diagnostic: Reported the tension magnitude 12,000 N as 12 kW.

D.diagnostic: Computed average power over the 3 seconds P_avg = 1/2 * P_inst = 36 kW instead of instantaneous power.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the formula for the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by a force vector?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Instantaneous power is the scalar dot product of force and instantaneous velocity: $P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$. When force and velocity are parallel, $P = F v$.

progressive_hints.title: Dynamic Tension Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the tension $T$ in the cable when the elevator accelerates upward at $a = 2\text{ m/s}^2$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By Newton's second law: $T - Mg = Ma \implies T = M(g + a) = 1000(10 + 2) = 12{,}000\text{ N}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the velocity at $t = 3\text{ s}$, and what is the resulting power product $T v$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Velocity: $v = u + at = 0 + 2(3) = 6\text{ m/s}$. Instantaneous power: $P = T v = 12{,}000\text{ N} \times 6\text{ m/s} = 72{,}000\text{ W} = 72\text{ kW}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Elevator of $M = 1000\text{ kg}$ accelerates upward at $2\text{ m/s}^2$ from rest. Goal: find instantaneous power of cable tension at $t = 3\text{ s}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Free-body diagram of elevator: upward tension $T$, downward gravity $Mg$. Kinematics: acceleration $a = 2\text{ m/s}^2$, $u = 0$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: 1) Dynamic tension: $\Sigma F_y = M a \implies T - Mg = Ma \implies T = M(g + a)$. 2) Velocity: $v(t) = at$. 3) Instantaneous power: $P(t) = T \cdot v(t)$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Tension: $T = 1000(10 + 2) = 12{,}000\text{ N}$. Velocity at $t = 3\text{ s}$: $v = 2 \times 3 = 6\text{ m/s}$. Power: $P = 12{,}000 \times 6 = 72{,}000\text{ W} = 72\text{ kW}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: At $t = 3\text{ s}$, the motor delivers $72\text{ kW}$ of electrical-to-mechanical power: $60\text{ kW}$ goes into overcoming gravity, and $12\text{ kW}$ goes into increasing the cab's kinetic energy.

derivation_steps: Equation of motion: $T - Mg = Ma$.
Solve for cable tension: $T = M(g + a) = 1000\text{ kg} \times (10 + 2)\text{ m/s}^2 = 12{,}000\text{ N}$.
Kinematic velocity at $t = 3\text{ s}$: $v = at = (2\text{ m/s}^2)(3\text{ s}) = 6\text{ m/s}$.
Instantaneous power formula: $P = T v$.
Calculate power: $P = 12{,}000\text{ N} \times 6\text{ m/s} = 72{,}000\text{ W} = 72\text{ kW}$.

limiting_cases.expected: v -> 0 => P -> 0 kW (Zero instantaneous power at start)

independent_check.quick_check: Work done as function of time: $W(t) = T s(t) = T \left(\frac{1}{2}at^2\right) = \frac{1}{2}M(g+a)a t^2$. Differentiate with respect to time: $P(t) = \frac{dW}{dt} = M(g+a)a t = 1000(12)(2)(3) = 72{,}000\text{ W}$. Exact match.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Energy rate partition check: $\frac{dE}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(U + K) = Mg\frac{dy}{dt} + \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{1}{2}M v^2\right) = Mg v + M v a = M(g + a) v = 1000(12)(6) = 72{,}000\text{ W}$. Power balance verified.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT confuse instantaneous power $P(t) = 72\text{ kW}$ with average power over the interval $P_{\text{avg}} = W/t = 36\text{ kW}$.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-08 (Power as Rate of Energy Transfer)

questions.stem: A simple pendulum consists of a bob of mass $m$ attached to a light inextensible string of length $L = 2\text{ m}$. The bob is released from rest when the string makes an angle $\theta_0 = 60^\circ$ with the vertical. What is the speed of the bob and the tension in the string as it passes through the lowest vertical point of its swing? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with datum at lowest point

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesizing vertical elevation drop h = L(1 - cos 60°) = 1 m with energy conservation v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(20) m/s and circular dynamics tension T = mg + m v^2 / L = 2 mg.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires coupling conservation of energy with circular centripetal force constraint.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Drop h = L(1 - cos 60°) = 2(1 - 0.5) = 1 m. Energy conservation: v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 * 10 * 1) = sqrt(20) ≈ 4.47 m/s. Centripetal dynamics at bottom: T - mg = m v^2 / L => T = mg + m(20)/2 = mg + 10m = 2 mg.

B.diagnostic: Equated tension to static weight T = mg, omitting the required centripetal acceleration force m v^2 / L.

C.diagnostic: Used h = L = 2 m (assuming 90° release): v = sqrt(40) m/s, T = 3 mg.

D.diagnostic: Used h = L cos(60°) = 1 m but miscalculated velocity as 2 m/s.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the vertical height $h$ through which the pendulum bob descends from angle $\theta_0 = 60^\circ$ to the lowest point?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: From geometry, the height of release above the lowest point is $h = L - L\cos\theta_0 = L(1 - \cos\theta_0) = 2(1 - \cos 60^\circ) = 2(1 - 0.5) = 1.0\text{ m}$.

progressive_hints.title: Conservation of Energy Speed
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the speed of the bob at the lowest point by conservation of mechanical energy?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Loss in gravitational potential energy equals gain in kinetic energy: $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \implies v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(10)(1)} = \sqrt{20}\text{ m/s} \approx 4.47\text{ m/s}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the string tension $T$ at the lowest point using Newton's second law for circular motion?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: At the lowest point, the net upward force provides the centripetal acceleration: $T - mg = \frac{mv^2}{L}$. Substituting $v^2 = 2gh = 20\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$ and $L = 2\text{ m}$ gives $T = mg + \frac{m(20)}{2} = mg + 10m = mg + mg = 2mg$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Pendulum of length $L = 2\text{ m}$ released from rest at $\theta_0 = 60^\circ$. Goal: find speed $v$ and string tension $T$ at the bottom.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Datum $y = 0$ at lowest point. Bob released at $y_1 = L(1 - \cos 60^\circ)$. At bottom: $y_2 = 0$. FBD at bottom: upward tension $T$, downward gravity $mg$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: 1) Mechanical energy conservation: $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. 2) Radial dynamics at lowest point: $\Sigma F_r = m a_c \implies T - mg = \frac{mv^2}{L}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $h = 2(1 - 0.5) = 1.0\text{ m}$. Speed: $v = \sqrt{2(10)(1.0)} = \sqrt{20}\text{ m/s} \approx 4.47\text{ m/s}$. Tension: $T = mg + \frac{m(20)}{2} = mg + 10m = 2mg$ (since $g = 10$).
reasoning_ladder.interpret: At the bottom, the string tension must support both the static weight ($mg$) and provide the centripetal acceleration ($m v^2/L = mg$), resulting in double the static weight ($2mg$).

derivation_steps: Vertical drop: $h = L(1 - \cos\theta_0) = 2(1 - \cos 60^\circ) = 2(0.5) = 1.0\text{ m}$.
Conservation of mechanical energy: $mgh = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \implies v = \sqrt{2gh}$.
Substitute values: $v = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 1.0} = \sqrt{20}\text{ m/s} \approx 4.47\text{ m/s}$.
Equation of circular motion at lowest point: $T - mg = \frac{m v^2}{L}$.
Substitute $v^2 = 2gh$: $T = mg + \frac{m(2gh)}{L} = mg\left(1 + \frac{2h}{L}\right) = mg(1 + 2(1 - \cos\theta_0))$.

limiting_cases.expected: v -> 0 m/s, T = mg(3 - 2 cos 0) = mg(3 - 2) = mg (Static equilibrium)

questions.stem: A block of mass $m = 4\text{ kg}$ slides down a curved track of vertical height $H = 5\text{ m}$. Due to friction along the track, $50\text{ J}$ of mechanical energy is dissipated as thermal energy. With what speed does the block reach the bottom of the track? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Block sliding on rough curved track

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying the Work-Energy Theorem W_net = Delta K with W_g = mgh = 200 J and W_f = -50 J to find 1/2 m v^2 = 150 J => v = 5*sqrt(3) m/s.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires applying non-conservative work-energy accounting rather than pure potential-kinetic conversion.

B.diagnostic: Neglected friction entirely: v = sqrt(2gH) = sqrt(100) = 10.0 m/s.

C.diagnostic: Subtracted energy from velocity linearly: 10 - 2.5 = 7.5 m/s.

D.diagnostic: Divided remaining energy by 6 or miscalculated sqrt(75) as 5.0 m/s.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What does the Work-Energy Theorem state when both conservative gravity and non-conservative friction act on a body?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The net work done by ALL forces equals the change in kinetic energy: $W_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{gravity}} + W_{\text{friction}} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Energy Accounting Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the work done by gravity as the $4\text{ kg}$ block descends $5\text{ m}$, and what is the net work after friction?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Gravity work: $W_g = mgH = (4\text{ kg})(10\text{ m/s}^2)(5\text{ m}) = 200\text{ J}$. Friction dissipates $50\text{ J}$, so $W_f = -50\text{ J}$. Net work: $W_{\text{net}} = 200 - 50 = 150\text{ J}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the final speed $v$ obtained from $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 150\text{ J}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\frac{1}{2}(4\text{ kg}) v^2 = 150\text{ J} \implies 2 v^2 = 150 \implies v^2 = 75 \implies v = \sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s} \approx 8.66\text{ m/s}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Block of mass $4\text{ kg}$ slides down height $H = 5\text{ m}$. Friction dissipates $50\text{ J}$. Goal: find speed at the bottom.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Energy states: Initial state (top, at rest): $K_i = 0$, $U_i = mgH$. Final state (bottom): $K_f = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, $U_f = 0$. Friction work: $W_{\text{nc}} = -50\text{ J}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Work-Energy Theorem with non-conservative forces: $W_{\text{nc}} = \Delta E = (K_f + U_f) - (K_i + U_i) \implies -50 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - mgH$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Rearrange: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgH - 50 = 4(10)(5) - 50 = 200 - 50 = 150\text{ J}$. $\frac{1}{2}(4) v^2 = 150 \implies 2 v^2 = 150 \implies v = \sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s} \approx 8.66\text{ m/s}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Out of $200\text{ J}$ of gravitational potential energy released, $25\%$ ($50\text{ J}$) is dissipated into internal thermal energy, leaving $150\text{ J}$ as kinetic energy.

derivation_steps: Work-Energy theorem: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$.
Work done by gravity: $W_g = mgH = 4\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m/s}^2 \times 5\text{ m} = 200\text{ J}$.
Work done by friction: $W_f = -50\text{ J}$.
Net work: $W_{\text{net}} = 200\text{ J} - 50\text{ J} = 150\text{ J}$.
Equate to kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = 150\text{ J}$.
Solve for speed: $2 v^2 = 150 \implies v^2 = 75 \implies v = 5\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s} \approx 8.66\text{ m/s}$.

limiting_cases.condition: W_f -> 200 J (Maximum friction bringing block to rest at bottom)

independent_check.quick_check: Energy ratio: $K_f / U_i = 150 / 200 = 0.75$. Speed ratio: $v / v_{\text{ideal}} = \sqrt{0.75} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866$. $10 \times 0.866 = 8.66\text{ m/s}$. Exactly verified.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Friction force average along track length $s$: If track has length $s$, average friction is $\bar{f} = 50 / s$. Effective acceleration component: $\bar{a} = g(H/s) - \bar{f}/m$. $v^2 = 2 \bar{a} s = 2(gH - 50/m) = 2(50 - 12.5) = 2(37.5) = 75 \implies v = \sqrt{75}$. Matches identically.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT subtract thermal energy from velocity; energy must be subtracted before taking the square root ($v = \sqrt{2(E - Q)/m}$, NOT $v = \sqrt{2E/m} - \dots$).
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-03 (Work-Energy Theorem)

questions.stem: A particle of mass $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$ is released from rest at the rim of a smooth hemispherical bowl of radius $R = 1.8\text{ m}$. What is the normal reaction force exerted by the bowl on the particle when it passes through the lowest point of the bowl? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Particle sliding on smooth hemispherical surface

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling energy conservation v^2 = 2gR and circular normal force N = mg + m v^2 / R = 3 mg = 3 * 0.5 * 10 = 15 N.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires coupling circular normal constraint dynamics with gravitational potential conversion.

A.diagnostic: Correct: From rim to bottom, vertical drop is R. Conservation of energy: 1/2 m v^2 = mgR => v^2 = 2gR. At the bottom, radial acceleration is centripetal: N - mg = m v^2 / R => N = mg + 2mg = 3mg = 3(0.5)(10) = 15 N.

B.diagnostic: Used static equilibrium N = mg = 0.5 * 10 = 5 N, omitting the centripetal acceleration force 2mg.

C.diagnostic: Only computed the centripetal force: m v^2 / R = 2mg = 10 N, forgetting to add the static weight mg.

D.diagnostic: Used 4mg = 20 N.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the speed squared $v^2$ of the particle at the bottom of the bowl of radius $R$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Because the bowl is frictionless, mechanical energy is conserved. Releasing from the rim corresponds to a vertical descent of height $h = R$. Therefore, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgR \implies v^2 = 2gR$.

progressive_hints.title: Radial Dynamics Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What forces act in the radial vertical direction at the bottom, and what is the equation of motion?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: At the bottom, upward normal force $N$ and downward gravity $mg$ act along the radius. The net upward force provides the centripetal acceleration: $N - mg = \frac{mv^2}{R}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the normal force $N$ expressed as a multiple of $mg$, and what is its value for $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Substitute $v^2 = 2gR$: $N = mg + \frac{m(2gR)}{R} = mg + 2mg = 3mg$. With $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$ and $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$: $N = 3 \times 0.5 \times 10 = 15\text{ N}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Particle of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ released from rim of smooth bowl of radius $R = 1.8\text{ m}$. Goal: find normal force $N$ at the bottom.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Origin at center of hemispherical bowl. Rim at $y = 0$, bottom at $y = -R$. Vertical descent $h = R$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: 1) Energy conservation: $mgR = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \implies v^2 = 2gR$. 2) Newton's second law along radial direction at bottom: $\Sigma F_r = N - mg = \frac{mv^2}{R}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $N = mg + \frac{m(2gR)}{R} = mg + 2mg = 3mg$. Substitute $m = 0.5\text{ kg}, g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$: $N = 3(0.5)(10) = 15\text{ N}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Remarkably, the normal force $N = 3mg$ at the bottom is completely independent of the radius $R$ of the bowl; it is always exactly three times the weight of the particle.

derivation_steps: Vertical displacement from rim to bottom: $h = R$.
Conservation of mechanical energy: $mgh = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \implies v^2 = 2gR$.
Centripetal acceleration at bottom: $a_c = \frac{v^2}{R} = \frac{2gR}{R} = 2g$.
Radial force balance at lowest point: $N - mg = m a_c = 2mg$.
Solve for normal reaction force: $N = mg + 2mg = 3mg$.
Insert values: $N = 3 \times 0.5\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m/s}^2 = 15\text{ N}$.

independent_check.quick_check: Radius independence check: $R = 1.8\text{ m}$ canceled out identically in $\frac{2gR}{R} = 2g$. Result depends only on mass $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$ and $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$: $3 \times 5 = 15\text{ N}$. Invariant confirmed.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: General formula for release from angle $\theta_0$ to vertical: $N = mg(3\cos\theta - 2\cos\theta_0)$. For rim release, $\theta_0 = 90^\circ$ ($\cos 90^\circ = 0$), and at bottom $\theta = 0^\circ$ ($\cos 0^\circ = 1$): $N = mg(3(1) - 2(0)) = 3mg$. Exactly matches.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT divide by or worry about the bowl radius $R = 1.8\text{ m}$; the speed squared grows linearly with $R$ while centripetal acceleration divides by $R$, making normal force scale-invariant.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-07 (Mechanical Energy Conservation & Turning Points)

questions.stem: A particle of mass $m = 1\text{ kg}$ moves in a conservative 1D potential field defined by $U(x) = x^3 - 3x$, where $x$ is in meters and $U$ is in Joules (Figure WEP-13). Which of the following statements correctly identifies the positions and stability classifications of the equilibrium points?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Particle moving in 1D cubic potential well

options.A: Stable equilibrium at $x = +1\text{ m}$, Unstable equilibrium at $x = -1\text{ m}$
options.B: Stable equilibrium at $x = -1\text{ m}$, Unstable equilibrium at $x = +1\text{ m}$
options.C: Both $x = +1\text{ m}$ and $x = -1\text{ m}$ are stable equilibria

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating dU/dx = 3(x^2 - 1) = 0 to identify equilibria at x = ±1 m, and using the second derivative d^2U/dx^2 = 6x to classify x = +1 m as stable (minimum) and x = -1 m as unstable (maximum).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires representation and classification of potential well curvature and restorative forces.

A.diagnostic: Correct: dU/dx = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 => x = ±1 m. d^2U/dx^2 = 6x. At x = +1: d^2U/dx^2 = +6 > 0 (potential minimum => stable). At x = -1: d^2U/dx^2 = -6 < 0 (potential maximum => unstable).

B.diagnostic: Inverted stability criteria: assumed maximum was stable and minimum was unstable.

C.diagnostic: Claimed both extrema are stable, ignoring that a local maximum has negative curvature.

D.diagnostic: Confused the inflection point at x = 0 (where d^2U/dx^2 = 0) with a neutral equilibrium (where dU/dx must be zero).

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the condition for a particle to be in mechanical equilibrium in a conservative potential field?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Equilibrium occurs where the net conservative force vanishes: $F = -\frac{dU}{dx} = 0 \implies \frac{dU}{dx} = 0$. This corresponds to the horizontal tangent points (extrema) of the potential curve $U(x)$.

progressive_hints.title: First Derivative Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are the roots of $\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$ for $U(x) = x^3 - 3x$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\frac{dU}{dx} = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x^2 - 1) = 0 \implies x^2 = 1 \implies x = +1\text{ m}$ and $x = -1\text{ m}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How does the second derivative $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2}$ determine the stability of each equilibrium point?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Curvature test: $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = 6x$. At $x = +1\text{ m}$: $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = +6 > 0$ (potential well / minimum $\implies$ STABLE). At $x = -1\text{ m}$: $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = -6 < 0$ (potential peak / barrier $\implies$ UNSTABLE).

reasoning_ladder.understand: Potential energy $U(x) = x^3 - 3x$. Goal: determine equilibrium points and classify their stability.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Potential curve $U(x)$ vs $x$. Force function: $F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: 1) Equilibrium: $F(x) = 0 \iff \frac{dU}{dx} = 0$. 2) Stability condition: Stable if potential is a local minimum ($\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} > 0$), Unstable if local maximum ($\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} < 0$).
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $\frac{dU}{dx} = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 \implies x = \pm 1\text{ m}$. $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = 6x$. For $x = +1$: $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = +6 > 0 \implies$ Stable. For $x = -1$: $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = -6 < 0 \implies$ Unstable.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Near $x = +1\text{ m}$, small displacements produce restoring forces back toward $x = 1$. Near $x = -1\text{ m}$, small displacements produce repelling forces that push the particle away from $x = -1$.

derivation_steps: Force relation: $F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx}$.
First derivative: $\frac{dU}{dx} = 3x^2 - 3$.
Set $\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$: $3(x^2 - 1) = 0 \implies x = +1\text{ m}$ and $x = -1\text{ m}$.
Second derivative: $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = 6x$.
Evaluate at $x = +1\text{ m}$: $\left.\frac{d^2U}{dx^2}\right|_{x=1} = +6 > 0 \implies$ Local minimum $\implies$ Stable equilibrium.
Evaluate at $x = -1\text{ m}$: $\left.\frac{d^2U}{dx^2}\right|_{x=-1} = -6 < 0 \implies$ Local maximum $\implies$ Unstable equilibrium.

independent_check.quick_check: At $x = 1.1\text{ m}$ (displaced right of $+1$): $F = -(3(1.21) - 3) = -0.63\text{ N} < 0$ (force pushes LEFT toward $+1$). At $x = 0.9\text{ m}$: $F = -(3(0.81) - 3) = +0.57\text{ N} > 0$ (force pushes RIGHT toward $+1$). Restoring force confirmed $\implies$ Stable.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: At $x = -0.9\text{ m}$ (displaced right of $-1$): $F = -(3(0.81) - 3) = +0.57\text{ N} > 0$ (force pushes further right away from $-1$). Destabilizing force confirmed $\implies$ Unstable.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT confuse the inflection point at $x = 0$ with an equilibrium; at $x = 0$, $dU/dx = -3 \ne 0$, so there is an active force of $+3\text{ N}$.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-06 (Conservative Force as Negative Potential Gradient)

questions.stem: A box of mass $m = 10\text{ kg}$ is gently placed with zero initial horizontal velocity onto a long horizontal conveyor belt moving at a constant speed $v = 6\text{ m/s}$ (Figure WEP-14). The coefficient of kinetic friction between the box and the belt is $\mu_k = 0.3$. In the ground (lab) frame of reference, what is the work done by kinetic friction on the box during the slipping phase until it moves synchronously with the belt? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Box placed onto moving conveyor belt

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Justifying that forward kinetic friction accelerates the box from rest in the lab frame, doing POSITIVE work W = Delta K = 1/2 m v^2 = +180 J.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires refutation of the universal misconception that friction can only perform negative work.

A.diagnostic: Correct: In the lab frame, the box starts from rest (u = 0) and reaches velocity v = 6 m/s. The only horizontal force acting on the box is forward kinetic friction. By the Work-Energy Theorem: W_f = Delta K = 1/2 m v^2 - 0 = 1/2(10)(36) = +180 J.

B.diagnostic: Universal friction misconception: assumed friction can only do negative work, reporting -180 J.

C.diagnostic: Reported the work done by the motor driving the belt: W_belt = f_k * d_belt = 30 * 12 = +360 J.

D.diagnostic: Claimed zero work because the box eventually rides passively with the belt.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: In what direction does the kinetic friction force act on the box, and in what direction is the box displaced in the lab frame?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Because the belt moves forward beneath the stationary box, relative sliding of the belt is forward, so friction on the box acts FORWARD. The box accelerates forward and moves forward. Because force and displacement are in the SAME direction, friction does POSITIVE work on the box!

progressive_hints.title: Work-Energy Theorem Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the initial and final kinetic energy of the box in the lab frame?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Initial kinetic energy: $K_i = 0$ (placed with zero initial velocity). Final kinetic energy: $K_f = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(10\text{ kg})(6\text{ m/s})^2 = 180\text{ J}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: By the Work-Energy Theorem, what is the work done on the box by the net horizontal force?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The only horizontal force on the box is friction: $W_f = \Delta K = K_f - K_i = 180\text{ J} - 0 = +180\text{ J}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Box of $m = 10\text{ kg}$ placed from rest onto belt moving at $v = 6\text{ m/s}$ with $\mu_k = 0.3$. Goal: find work done by friction on the box in the lab frame.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Inertial lab frame: $+x$ along belt direction. Friction force on box: $f_k = \mu_k mg = 0.3(10)(10) = 30\text{ N}$ in $+x$ direction.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Work-Energy Theorem in lab frame: $W_{\text{fric}} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Initial state: $u = 0 \implies K_i = 0$. Final state: $v = 6\text{ m/s} \implies K_f = \frac{1}{2}(10)(6^2) = 180\text{ J}$. Thus $W_{\text{fric}} = +180\text{ J}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: While the total system dissipates mechanical energy into heat ($Q = 180\text{ J}$), the kinetic friction force does POSITIVE work ($+180\text{ J}$) on the box itself, accelerating it from rest.

derivation_steps: Kinetic friction on box: $f_k = \mu_k mg = 0.3 \times 10\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m/s}^2 = 30\text{ N}$ directed forward.
Acceleration of box: $a = f_k / m = 30 / 10 = 3\text{ m/s}^2$.
Time to reach belt speed: $t = v / a = 6 / 3 = 2\text{ s}$.
Displacement of box in lab frame: $d_{\text{box}} = \frac{1}{2} a t^2 = \frac{1}{2}(3)(2^2) = 6\text{ m}$.
Direct work calculation: $W_f = f_k \times d_{\text{box}} = 30\text{ N} \times 6\text{ m} = +180\text{ J}$.

independent_check.quick_check: Belt displacement in 2 seconds: $d_{\text{belt}} = v t = 6 \times 2 = 12\text{ m}$. Work done by motor on belt: $W_{\text{motor}} = f_k d_{\text{belt}} = 30 \times 12 = +360\text{ J}$. Work received by box: $+180\text{ J}$. Heat dissipated: $Q = 360 - 180 = 180\text{ J}$. Perfect energy balance.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Relative sliding displacement: $d_{\text{rel}} = d_{\text{belt}} - d_{\text{box}} = 12 - 6 = 6\text{ m}$. Dissipated heat: $Q = f_k d_{\text{rel}} = 30 \times 6 = 180\text{ J}$. Energy conservation verified.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT believe friction always does negative work; whenever friction causes a body to accelerate in the direction of motion (such as walking, driving, or conveyor belts), it does positive work in the lab frame.

questions.stem: A high-speed train encounters aerodynamic drag force proportional to the square of its speed, $F_{\text{drag}} = c v^2$, where $c$ is a constant (Figure WEP-15). When cruising at a steady speed of $v_1 = 180\text{ km/h}$, the train's locomotive engine delivers a power output of $P_1 = 2000\text{ kW}$. What power output $P_2$ must the engine deliver to cruise steadily at double the speed, $v_2 = 360\text{ km/h}$?

idealizations: Pure aerodynamic drag F_drag = c v^2

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling cubic power scaling P = F * v = (c v^2) * v = c v^3, showing that doubling speed multiplies required power by 2^3 = 8 => 16,000 kW.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires functional power scaling modeling under velocity-dependent dissipative forces.

A.diagnostic: Correct: P = F * v = (c * v^2) * v = c * v^3. Power scales with the cube of speed: P2 / P1 = (v2 / v1)^3 = (2)^3 = 8. Thus P2 = 8 * 2000 kW = 16,000 kW.

B.diagnostic: Assumed power scales with drag force (quadratically): P2 = 4 * 2000 = 8000 kW, forgetting the extra velocity factor in P = F * v.

C.diagnostic: Assumed power scales linearly with speed: P2 = 2 * 2000 = 4000 kW.

D.diagnostic: Used 4th power scaling: 2^4 * 2000 = 32,000 kW.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the relationship between engine power $P$, resistive force $F_{\text{drag}}$, and cruising speed $v$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: To cruise at constant speed, the engine must supply a thrust force equal and opposite to drag: $F = F_{\text{drag}} = c v^2$. The mechanical power required is $P = F v = (c v^2) v = c v^3$.

progressive_hints.title: Cubic Scaling Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How does power scale when speed is increased by a factor of 2?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Because $P \propto v^3$, doubling the speed increases the power requirement by a factor of $2^3 = 8$: $\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right)^3 = 2^3 = 8$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the required power output $P_2$ when $P_1 = 2000\text{ kW}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $P_2 = 8 \times P_1 = 8 \times 2000\text{ kW} = 16{,}000\text{ kW}$ ($16\text{ MW}$).

reasoning_ladder.understand: Train cruises against drag $F = c v^2$. At $v_1 = 180\text{ km/h}$, $P_1 = 2000\text{ kW}$. Goal: find $P_2$ at $v_2 = 360\text{ km/h}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Equilibrium condition at constant speed: $F_{\text{thrust}} = F_{\text{drag}} = c v^2$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Power relation: $P = F v = c v^3$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Speed ratio: $\frac{v_2}{v_1} = \frac{360}{180} = 2$. Power ratio: $\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right)^3 = 2^3 = 8$. $P_2 = 8 \times 2000\text{ kW} = 16{,}000\text{ kW}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: A modest doubling of speed requires an eight-fold increase in locomotive power; aerodynamic drag becomes brutally dominant at high speeds.

derivation_steps: Drag force: $F = c v^2$.
Power definition: $P = F v = (c v^2) v = c v^3$.
Initial state: $P_1 = c v_1^3$.
Calculate power: $P_2 = 8 \times 2000\text{ kW} = 16{,}000\text{ kW}$.

independent_check.quick_check: Convert to SI units: $v_1 = 180\text{ km/h} = 50\text{ m/s}$. Drag force: $F_1 = P_1 / v_1 = (2 \times 10^6\text{ W}) / 50\text{ m/s} = 40{,}000\text{ N}$. At $v_2 = 100\text{ m/s}$, drag quadruples: $F_2 = 4 \times 40{,}000 = 160{,}000\text{ N}$. Power: $P_2 = F_2 v_2 = 160{,}000 \times 100 = 16{,}000{,}000\text{ W} = 16{,}000\text{ kW}$. Exact match.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Logarithmic differentiation: $\frac{dP}{P} = 3\frac{dv}{v}$. Finite scaling factor $(1 + 1)^3 = 8$. Verified.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT confuse drag force scaling ($F \propto v^2$) with power scaling ($P \propto v^3$); you must multiply the force by another factor of velocity to get power.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-08 (Power as Rate of Energy Transfer)

questions.stem: A particle of mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ is initially at rest at the origin ($x = 0$). It is subjected to a position-dependent net force directed along the $+x$-axis given by $F(x) = (6x^2 + 4x)\text{ N}$, where $x$ is in meters. What is the kinetic energy of the particle when it reaches position $x = 3\text{ m}$?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating the definite integral W = int_0^3 (6x^2 + 4x) dx = [2x^3 + 2x^2]_0^3 = 54 + 18 = 72 J and equating to kinetic energy gain.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires polynomial integration calculus rather than unintegrated algebraic substitution.

B.diagnostic: Evaluated force at endpoint F(3) = 6(9) + 4(3) = 54 + 12 = 66 N and reported it directly as 66 J.

C.diagnostic: Multiplied endpoint force by distance: F(3) * x = 66 * 3 = 198 J, or miscalculated as 144 J.

D.diagnostic: Divided the integral result by 2 yielding 36 J.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What theorem links the work done by a variable force $F(x)$ to the particle's kinetic energy?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By the Work-Energy Theorem, the change in kinetic energy from rest is equal to the integral of the net force over displacement: $K = W = \int_{0}^{x} F(x') dx'$.

progressive_hints.title: Calculus Antiderivative Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the antiderivative of $F(x) = 6x^2 + 4x$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\int (6x^2 + 4x) dx = 6\left(\frac{x^3}{3}\right) + 4\left(\frac{x^2}{2}\right) = 2x^3 + 2x^2$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the value of $[2x^3 + 2x^2]$ evaluated from $x = 0$ to $x = 3\text{ m}$?

reasoning_ladder.understand: Particle of mass $2\text{ kg}$ released from rest at $x = 0$. Net force $F(x) = 6x^2 + 4x$. Goal: find kinetic energy at $x = 3\text{ m}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Kinematics in 1D: $u = 0 \implies K_i = 0$. $F(x)$ along positive x.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Work-Energy Theorem: $K(x) - 0 = \int_0^x F(x') dx'$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Because the particle started from rest, the entire $72\text{ J}$ of work performed by the variable force resides as kinetic energy in the particle ($v = \sqrt{72}\text{ m/s} \approx 8.49\text{ m/s}$).

derivation_steps: Work-Energy theorem: $K = \int_0^3 F(x) dx$.
Substitute force function: $K = \int_0^3 (6x^2 + 4x) dx$.
Compute antiderivative: $\int (6x^2 + 4x) dx = 2x^3 + 2x^2$.

independent_check.quick_check: Average force over interval: $\bar{F} = K / \Delta x = 72 / 3 = 24\text{ N}$. Force values: $F(0) = 0\text{ N}$, $F(3) = 6(9) + 4(3) = 66\text{ N}$. Average value $24\text{ N}$ strictly satisfies $0 < 24 < 66$. Validated.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Velocity integration check: $m v \frac{dv}{dx} = F(x) \implies \int_0^v m v' dv' = \int_0^3 (6x^2 + 4x) dx \implies \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = 72\text{ J}$. Differential chain rule verifies theorem directly.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT evaluate $F(3)$ and multiply by 3; force changes continuously with position from $0$ to $66\text{ N}$.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-02 (Work by Variable Forces & Spring Integration)

questions.stem: A block of mass $M = 2\text{ kg}$ is dropped from a height $h = 0.60\text{ m}$ above the top of a vertical, uncompressed ideal spring of stiffness $k = 400\text{ N/m}$. The block hits the spring and adheres to it, compressing the spring by a maximum distance $x_{\text{max}}$. What is the value of $x_{\text{max}}$? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with datum at uncompressed spring top

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling energy conservation Mg(h + x) = 1/2 k x^2 including the additional descent x during compression, solving the quadratic to find x_max = 0.30 m.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires coupled potential well modeling and complete gravitational descent accounting.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Total vertical drop from release to maximum compression is h + x. Energy conservation: M*g*(h + x) = 1/2 k x^2 => 20(0.60 + x) = 200 x^2 => 200 x^2 - 20 x - 12 = 0 => 50 x^2 - 5 x - 3 = 0 => (10x - 3)(5x + 1) = 0 => x = 0.30 m.

B.diagnostic: Neglected the extra descent during compression: solved M*g*h = 1/2 k x^2 => 12 = 200 x^2 => x ≈ 0.245 m or crudely estimated 0.15 m.

C.diagnostic: Equated compression to initial drop height: 0.45 m.

D.diagnostic: Dropped the linear term: 200 x^2 = 8 => x = 0.20 m.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the TOTAL vertical descent of the block from its initial release point to the lowest point of maximum spring compression?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The block falls through free distance $h = 0.60\text{ m}$ to reach the spring, and then descends an ADDITIONAL distance $x_{\text{max}}$ while compressing the spring. The total vertical descent is $H_{\text{total}} = h + x_{\text{max}}$.

progressive_hints.title: Energy Balance Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What equation expresses conservation of mechanical energy between release and maximum compression?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: At release, $K_i = 0$. At maximum compression, $K_f = 0$. Total gravitational potential energy lost equals elastic potential energy gained: $Mg(h + x_{\text{max}}) = \frac{1}{2} k x_{\text{max}}^2$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What quadratic equation results from inserting $M = 2\text{ kg}, g = 10\text{ m/s}^2, h = 0.60\text{ m},$ and $k = 400\text{ N/m}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $2(10)(0.60 + x) = \frac{1}{2}(400)x^2 \implies 20(0.60 + x) = 200x^2 \implies 12 + 20x = 200x^2 \implies 50x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0$. Factoring gives $(10x - 3)(5x + 1) = 0 \implies x_{\text{max}} = 0.30\text{ m}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ dropped from $h = 0.60\text{ m}$ onto vertical spring of $k = 400\text{ N/m}$. Goal: find maximum compression $x_{\text{max}}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Datum at uncompressed spring top ($y = 0$). Release at $y_1 = +0.60\text{ m}$. Lowest point at $y_2 = -x_{\text{max}}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Mechanical energy conservation: $\Delta E = 0 \implies \Delta K + \Delta U_g + \Delta U_s = 0$. With $K_1 = K_2 = 0$, $Mg(h + x) = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $20(0.60 + x) = 200x^2 \implies 200x^2 - 20x - 12 = 0$. Divide by 4: $50x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0$. Factor: $(10x - 3)(5x + 1) = 0$. Physical positive root: $x = \frac{3}{10} = 0.30\text{ m}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: At maximum compression ($0.30\text{ m}$), gravitational potential energy lost is $20 \times 0.90 = 18\text{ J}$, which perfectly balances stored spring energy $\frac{1}{2}(400)(0.30^2) = 18\text{ J}$.

derivation_steps: Establish datum at uncompressed top of spring ($y = 0$).
Total gravitational height lost: $H = h + x$.
Loss in gravitational potential energy: $\Delta U_g = Mg(h + x)$.
Gain in elastic potential energy: $\Delta U_s = \frac{1}{2} k x^2$.
Equate energies ($K_i = K_f = 0$): $Mg(h + x) = \frac{1}{2} k x^2$.
Substitute values: $2(10)(0.60 + x) = 200 x^2 \implies 200 x^2 - 20 x - 12 = 0$.
Divide by 4: $50 x^2 - 5 x - 3 = 0$.
Select positive physical root: $x = 0.30\text{ m}$.

limiting_cases.expected: Mg x = 1/2 k x^2 => x = 2Mg/k = 2(20)/400 = 0.10 m (Twice static equilibrium)

independent_check.quick_check: Energy balance check at $x = 0.30\text{ m}$: $\Delta U_g = 2(10)(0.60 + 0.30) = 20(0.90) = 18\text{ J}$. $\Delta U_s = \frac{1}{2}(400)(0.30)^2 = 200(0.09) = 18\text{ J}$. Identical match with zero residual.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Static equilibrium compression: $x_{\text{eq}} = Mg/k = 20/400 = 0.05\text{ m}$. Speed at equilibrium position ($x = 0.05\text{ m}$): $v^2 = 2g(h + x_{\text{eq}}) - \frac{k x_{\text{eq}}^2}{M} = 2(10)(0.65) - \frac{400(0.0025)}{2} = 13 - 0.5 = 12.5\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$. Amplitude of oscillation: $A = \sqrt{x_{\text{eq}}^2 + v^2/\omega^2} = \sqrt{0.0025 + 12.5/200} = \sqrt{0.0025 + 0.0625} = \sqrt{0.065} = 0.25495\text{ m} \dots$ Total compression $x_{\text{max}} = x_{\text{eq}} + A = 0.30\text{ m}$. Consistent.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT forget the term $Mgx$; gravity continues doing positive work while the spring compresses, increasing the maximum compression.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-05 (Gravitational & Elastic Potential Energy Wells)

questions.stem: A particle of mass $m = 0.1\text{ kg}$ is released from rest at the top edge of a smooth vertical circular track (spherical dome) of radius $R = 1.0\text{ m}$. At what angle $\theta$ from the upward vertical does the particle fly off (lose contact with) the outer surface of the track? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Particle sliding on convex spherical dome
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with origin at sphere center

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Justifying the loss-of-contact constraint N = 0 where mg cos(theta) = m v^2 / R, coupled with energy conservation 1/2 m v^2 = mgR(1 - cos(theta)), to prove cos(theta) = 2/3.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires justification of normal constraint vanishing on a convex surface.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Normal force N = mg*cos(theta) - m*v^2/R. Contact lost when N = 0 => v^2 = g*R*cos(theta). Energy conservation: 1/2 m v^2 = mgR(1 - cos(theta)) => v^2 = 2gR(1 - cos(theta)). Equating gives g*R*cos(theta) = 2gR(1 - cos(theta)) => 3 cos(theta) = 2 => cos(theta) = 2/3 => theta ≈ 48.2°.

B.diagnostic: Assumed particle leaves when height drops by R/2 (cos theta = 1/2 => theta = 60°).

C.diagnostic: Guessed 45° by symmetry.

D.diagnostic: Miscalculated factor as cos(theta) = 1/3 => 70.5°.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What mathematical condition defines the exact instant a particle flies off a surface?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: A surface can only push, never pull ($N \ge 0$). The particle loses contact with the surface at the exact instant the normal contact force drops to zero: $N = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Radial Force Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the radial equation of motion for the particle at angle $\theta$ from the vertical?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The component of gravity pointing inward toward the center is $mg\cos\theta$. By Newton's second law: $mg\cos\theta - N = \frac{mv^2}{R}$. When $N = 0$, this yields $v^2 = gR\cos\theta$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is $v^2$ from conservation of mechanical energy, and what is the resulting equation for $\cos\theta$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Height fallen: $h = R - R\cos\theta = R(1 - \cos\theta)$. Energy conservation: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh \implies v^2 = 2gR(1 - \cos\theta)$. Equating gives $2gR(1 - \cos\theta) = gR\cos\theta \implies 2 - 2\cos\theta = \cos\theta \implies 3\cos\theta = 2 \implies \cos\theta = \frac{2}{3}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Particle released from top of smooth sphere of radius $R$. Goal: determine angle $\theta$ where it flies off.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Polar coordinates with origin at sphere center. Angle $\theta$ measured from upward vertical. FBD: gravity $mg$ downward, normal force $N$ radially outward.
reasoning_ladder.connect: 1) Radial equation of motion: $mg\cos\theta - N = \frac{mv^2}{R}$. 2) Loss of contact condition: $N = 0$. 3) Mechanical energy conservation: $\Delta K = -\Delta U \implies \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgR(1 - \cos\theta)$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: At $N = 0$: $v^2 = gR\cos\theta$. From energy: $v^2 = 2gR(1 - \cos\theta)$. Equate: $2gR(1 - \cos\theta) = gR\cos\theta \implies 2 - 2\cos\theta = \cos\theta \implies 3\cos\theta = 2 \implies \cos\theta = \frac{2}{3} \implies \theta = \arccos(2/3) \approx 48.19^\circ$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The particle leaves the surface after descending a vertical distance of $h = R(1 - 2/3) = R/3$. Beyond this angle, the curvature of a free-fall parabola is flatter than the sphere, so the particle launches into projectile flight.

derivation_steps: Vertical descent as a function of angle $\theta$: $h(\theta) = R(1 - \cos\theta)$.
Speed from conservation of energy: $v^2 = 2gh = 2gR(1 - \cos\theta)$.
Radial force balance on circular surface: $mg\cos\theta - N = \frac{m v^2}{R}$.
Condition for loss of contact: $N = 0 \implies mg\cos\theta = \frac{m v^2}{R} \implies v^2 = gR\cos\theta$.
Equate both expressions for $v^2$: $2gR(1 - \cos\theta) = gR\cos\theta$.
Divide by $gR$: $2(1 - \cos\theta) = \cos\theta \implies 2 - 2\cos\theta = \cos\theta$.
Solve for $\cos\theta$: $3\cos\theta = 2 \implies \cos\theta = \frac{2}{3}$.
Angle: $\theta = \arccos(2/3) \approx 48.2^\circ$.

independent_check.quick_check: At $\cos\theta = 2/3$, speed is $v = \sqrt{2gR(1/3)} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}gR}$. Normal component of gravity is $g_n = g\cos\theta = \frac{2}{3}g$. Required centripetal acceleration is $a_c = v^2/R = \frac{(2/3)gR}{R} = \frac{2}{3}g$. Since $a_c = g_n$, gravity exactly provides the centripetal acceleration with zero normal assistance ($N = 0$). Verified.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Vertical descent check: $h = R - R(2/3) = R/3 = 1.0 / 3 \approx 0.333\text{ m}$. Height above center: $y = 2R/3 \approx 0.667\text{ m}$. Exact integer fraction $2/3$.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT assume the particle stays on the sphere until the horizontal equator ($\theta = 90^\circ$); gravity cannot provide enough inward curvature past $\theta \approx 48.2^\circ$.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-07 (Mechanical Energy Conservation & Turning Points)
