questions.stem: A particle of mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ moves along the $+x$-axis under a 1D force $F(x)$ that varies with position as $F(x) = (12 - 3x)\text{ N}$, where $x$ is in meters (Figure WEP-19). If the particle is released from rest at $x = 0$, what is its maximum kinetic energy during the subsequent motion?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Identifying equilibrium at F(x) = 0 => x = 4 m where kinetic energy is maximal, and integrating work W = int_0^4 (12 - 3x) dx = 48 - 24 = 24 J.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires identifying the kinematic extremum landmark and integrating the force curve.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Maximum kinetic energy occurs when force drops to zero (equilibrium): 12 - 3x = 0 => x = 4 m. Beyond x = 4 m, force opposes motion and decelerates the particle. Work done from 0 to 4 m: K_max = int_0^4 (12 - 3x) dx = [12x - 1.5 x^2]_0^4 = 48 - 24 = 24 J.

B.diagnostic: Integrated to the turning point at x = 8 m (where K returns to 0) or forgot the negative integration term: 12 * 4 = 48 J.

C.diagnostic: Evaluated at x = 3 m yielding 36 - 13.5 = 22.5 J, miscalculated as 18 J.

D.diagnostic: Confused maximum force 12 N with energy 12 J.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: At what position along the trajectory does the kinetic energy reach its maximum value?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By the Work-Energy Theorem, $\frac{dK}{dx} = F(x)$. Kinetic energy increases as long as $F(x) > 0$. Therefore, kinetic energy is MAXIMAL where the force drops to zero: $F(x) = 0$ (the equilibrium position).

progressive_hints.title: Equilibrium Landmark Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: At what position $x$ is the force $F(x) = 12 - 3x$ equal to zero?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $12 - 3x = 0 \implies 3x = 12 \implies x = 4\text{ m}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the work done by $F(x)$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 4\text{ m}$?

reasoning_ladder.understand: Force $F(x) = 12 - 3x$. Released from rest at $x = 0$. Goal: find maximum kinetic energy $K_{\max}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Kinetic energy relation: $K(x) = \int_0^x F(x') dx'$. Extrema occur where $\frac{dK}{dx} = F(x) = 0$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: 1) Find equilibrium position: $12 - 3x = 0 \implies x = 4\text{ m}$. 2) Evaluate integral up to equilibrium.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: From $x = 0$ to $4\text{ m}$, the force accelerates the particle, building up $24\text{ J}$ of kinetic energy. Beyond $x = 4\text{ m}$, the force reverses direction, decelerating the particle to rest at the turning point $x = 8\text{ m}$.

derivation_steps: Condition for maximum kinetic energy: $\frac{dK}{dx} = F(x) = 0$.
Set force to zero: $12 - 3x = 0 \implies x = 4\text{ m}$.
Express kinetic energy from rest: $K_{\max} = \int_0^4 F(x) dx$.
Substitute force: $K_{\max} = \int_0^4 (12 - 3x) dx$.

independent_check.quick_check: Rewrite force as spring force: $F(x) = -3(x - 4)$. This is a simple harmonic oscillator with effective spring constant $k = 3\text{ N/m}$ centered at $x_0 = 4\text{ m}$. Release at $x = 0$ means amplitude is $A = |0 - 4| = 4\text{ m}$. Maximum kinetic energy is $\frac{1}{2} k A^2 = \frac{1}{2}(3)(4^2) = \frac{1}{2}(3)(16) = 24\text{ J}$. Exact match.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Triangular area check on $F-x$ plot: base from $x=0$ to $4\text{ m}$ is $4\text{ m}$, peak force at $x=0$ is $12\text{ N}$. Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 12 = 24\text{ J}$. Instant geometric verification.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT integrate to $x = 8\text{ m}$; at $x = 8\text{ m}$, the particle is at its turning point where kinetic energy is zero, not maximum.

questions.stem: A block of mass $m_1 = 3\text{ kg}$ moving at velocity $v_1 = 8\text{ m/s}$ along a smooth horizontal surface collides head-on and elastically with a stationary block of mass $m_2 = 5\text{ kg}$ equipped with an ideal massless bumper spring. What is the maximum elastic potential energy stored in the spring during the collision at the instant of maximum deformation?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two-block isolated collision system with spring interface

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesizing center-of-mass momentum conservation with relative kinetic energy reduction U_max = 1/2 * mu * v_rel^2 = 1/2 * (15/8) * 64 = 60 J.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires center-of-mass frame transformation or dual conservation coupling to identify maximum deformation.

A.diagnostic: Correct: At maximum compression, both blocks move with the common center-of-mass velocity v_cm = (m1*v1)/(m1+m2) = (3*8)/8 = 3 m/s. Initial kinetic energy K_i = 1/2(3)(64) = 96 J. Kinetic energy at max compression K_cm = 1/2(m1+m2)v_cm^2 = 1/2(8)(9) = 36 J. Stored elastic energy U_max = K_i - K_cm = 96 - 36 = 60 J.

B.diagnostic: Assumed all initial kinetic energy converts to spring energy: K_i = 1/2(3)(64) = 96 J, violating momentum conservation.

C.diagnostic: Reported the remaining kinetic energy of the center-of-mass K_cm = 36 J instead of the stored spring potential energy.

D.diagnostic: Used equal mass formula mu = m/2 = 1.5 kg yielding 48 J.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the kinematic relationship between the two blocks at the exact instant of maximum spring compression?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: At maximum spring compression, the distance between the blocks is neither decreasing nor increasing; they move with the EXACT SAME velocity, which must equal the velocity of the center of mass: $v_1 = v_2 = v_{\text{cm}}$.

progressive_hints.title: Center of Mass Velocity Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the center of mass velocity $v_{\text{cm}}$ of the two-block system?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By conservation of linear momentum: $v_{\text{cm}} = \frac{m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{(3\text{ kg})(8\text{ m/s}) + (5\text{ kg})(0)}{3 + 5} = \frac{24}{8} = 3\text{ m/s}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the stored spring energy $U_{\max} = K_{\text{initial}} - K_{\text{cm}}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Initial kinetic energy: $K_i = \frac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2 = \frac{1}{2}(3)(8^2) = 96\text{ J}$. Kinetic energy at maximum compression: $K_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2) v_{\text{cm}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}(8)(3^2) = 36\text{ J}$. Stored spring energy: $U_{\max} = 96 - 36 = 60\text{ J}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Block $m_1 = 3\text{ kg}$ at $v_1 = 8\text{ m/s}$ collides elastically with stationary $m_2 = 5\text{ kg}$ via bumper spring. Goal: find maximum stored spring energy $U_{\max}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Isolated 2-body system. Center of mass velocity $v_{\text{cm}}$. Reduced mass $\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: 1) Momentum conservation: total momentum $P = m_1 v_1$ is constant. 2) Koenig's theorem: total kinetic energy $K = K_{\text{cm}} + K_{\text{rel}}$, where $K_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{2}(m_1+m_2)v_{\text{cm}}^2$ is unalterable under internal forces. 3) At maximum compression, relative motion stops ($K_{\text{rel}} = 0$), so all relative kinetic energy converts into spring potential energy: $U_{\max} = K_{\text{rel}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Reduced mass: $\mu = \frac{3 \times 5}{3 + 5} = \frac{15}{8}\text{ kg}$. Relative velocity: $v_{\text{rel}} = 8 - 0 = 8\text{ m/s}$. Stored energy: $U_{\max} = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{15}{8}\right) (8^2) = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{15}{8}\right) (64) = \frac{15 \times 8}{2} = 60\text{ J}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Out of $96\text{ J}$ of initial kinetic energy, $36\text{ J}$ must remain as kinetic energy to conserve system momentum. The remaining $60\text{ J}$ is temporarily stored as elastic potential energy in the compressed spring.

derivation_steps: Total initial momentum: $P_{\text{tot}} = m_1 v_1 + m_2(0) = 3\text{ kg} \times 8\text{ m/s} = 24\text{ kg m/s}$.
Center of mass velocity: $v_{\text{cm}} = \frac{P_{\text{tot}}}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{24\text{ kg m/s}}{8\text{ kg}} = 3\text{ m/s}$.
Initial total kinetic energy: $K_i = \frac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2 = \frac{1}{2}(3)(8^2) = 96\text{ J}$.
Kinetic energy associated with center-of-mass motion: $K_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{2} (m_1 + m_2) v_{\text{cm}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}(8)(3^2) = 36\text{ J}$.
Conservation of total mechanical energy at maximum compression: $K_i = K_{\text{cm}} + U_{\max}$.
Solve for stored spring potential energy: $U_{\max} = K_i - K_{\text{cm}} = 96\text{ J} - 36\text{ J} = 60\text{ J}$.

limiting_cases.expected: mu -> m1 = 3 kg => U_max = 1/2(3)(64) = 96 J (All energy stored in spring)

independent_check.quick_check: Center-of-mass frame speeds: In CM frame, $u_1' = 8 - 3 = +5\text{ m/s}$, $u_2' = 0 - 3 = -3\text{ m/s}$. Relative kinetic energy: $K' = \frac{1}{2}m_1(u_1')^2 + \frac{1}{2}m_2(u_2')^2 = \frac{1}{2}(3)(25) + \frac{1}{2}(5)(9) = 37.5 + 22.5 = 60\text{ J}$. Exactly matches $U_{\max} = 60\text{ J}$.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Reduced mass formula: $U_{\max} = \frac{1}{2}\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{15}{8}\right)(64) = 15 \times 4 = 60\text{ J}$. Exact one-line verification.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT assume all $96\text{ J}$ converts into spring energy; total momentum cannot vanish, so the center of mass must keep moving with $36\text{ J}$ of kinetic energy.

questions.stem: A particle of mass $m$ is suspended from a fixed ceiling pivot by a light, inextensible string of length $L$ in a vertical plane. What minimum horizontal speed $u_{\text{min}}$ must be imparted to the particle at its lowest equilibrium position so that it successfully completes a full vertical circular loop without the string ever going slack?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesizing vertical radial circular acceleration condition at the zenith (T >= 0 => v_top^2 = gL) with total mechanical energy conservation across 2L descent to deduce u_min = sqrt(5gL).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires coordinating boundary constraint conditions with integral energy conservation across varying curvature.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Requiring string tension T >= 0 at the apex yields critical speed v_top = sqrt(gL). Applying mechanical energy conservation across vertical descent 2L gives u_min^2 = v_top^2 + 2g(2L) = gL + 4gL = 5gL, hence u_min = sqrt(5gL).

B.diagnostic: Assumes the particle only needs enough energy to reach the top with zero speed (v_top = 0, giving u = sqrt(4gL)). But for a flexible string, tension becomes zero and goes negative before reaching the zenith (T < 0 for v < sqrt(gL)), causing the particle to leave the circle and fall into a parabolic trajectory at height h = 5/3 L.

C.diagnostic: Corresponds to an intermediate launch speed where the particle reaches theta > 90 deg but slacks before reaching the top (at height h = 1/3 (u^2/g + L)).

D.diagnostic: Confuses the maximum tension difference between bottom and top (Delta T = 6mg) with the velocity coefficient inside the radical.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the physical condition at the very top of the vertical circle that prevents the inextensible string from collapsing or going slack?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The string remains taut as long as its tension is non-negative: $T \ge 0$. At the highest point (zenith), both gravity $mg$ and tension $T$ point downward toward the center: $T + mg = \frac{m v_{\text{top}}^2}{L}$. The critical threshold occurs when $T = 0$, giving $v_{\text{top}}^2 = g L$.

progressive_hints.title: Energy Accounting Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Why is mechanical energy conserved during the circular swing, and what is the potential energy change between bottom and top?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Tension acts perpendicular to displacement at every instant ($T \perp d\vec{r}$), so $W_T = 0$. Only conservative gravity does work. Setting potential energy $U = 0$ at the bottom, the height at the top is $2L$, so $U_{\text{top}} = mg(2L) = 2mgL$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How do you combine energy conservation with the critical apex speed to find the minimum launch speed $u_{\text{min}}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Equate total mechanical energy: $E_{\text{bottom}} = E_{\text{top}} \implies \frac{1}{2}m u_{\text{min}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}m v_{\text{top}}^2 + 2mgL$. Substitute $v_{\text{top}}^2 = gL$: $\frac{1}{2}m u_{\text{min}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}m(gL) + 2mgL = \frac{5}{2}mgL \implies u_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{5gL}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: A particle of mass $m$ suspended by string $L$ must loop vertically without slacking. Goal: find minimum horizontal speed $u_{\text{min}}$ at bottom.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Coordinates: Polar coordinates centered at pivot $O$. Bottom: $\theta = 0$, speed $u$. Top: $\theta = 180^\circ$, speed $v_{\text{top}}$, height $h = 2L$. Radial equation at top: $T + mg = m v_{\text{top}}^2 / L$. Slack condition: $T \ge 0$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Work done by tension is identically zero ($W_T = 0$). By conservation of mechanical energy: $E_{\text{bottom}} = E_{\text{top}} \implies \frac{1}{2}m u^2 = \frac{1}{2}m v_{\text{top}}^2 + mg(2L)$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Critical threshold at top: $T = 0 \implies v_{\text{top}}^2 = g L$. Substitute into energy conservation: $\frac{1}{2}m u^2 = \frac{1}{2}m(g L) + 2 m g L = \frac{5}{2} m g L \implies u_{\text{min}}^2 = 5 g L \implies u_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{5 g L}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: To complete the vertical circle on a string, kinetic energy at the bottom must be $\frac{5}{2}mgL$—$2mgL$ overcomes gravity, and $\frac{1}{2}mgL$ maintains the centrifugal inertia required to keep the string taut at the zenith.

derivation_steps: At zenith, radial equation: $T + mg = \frac{m v^2}{L}$.
Condition for string tautness: $T \ge 0 \implies v_{\text{top}}^2 \ge g L$.
Conservation of mechanical energy: $\frac{1}{2}m u^2 = \frac{1}{2}m v_{\text{top}}^2 + mg(2L)$.
Substitute $v_{\text{top}}^2 = g L$: $\frac{1}{2}m u_{\text{min}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}m g L + 2 m g L = \frac{5}{2}m g L$.
Solve for initial speed: $u_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{5 g L}$.

limiting_cases.condition: Rigid light rod instead of flexible string
limiting_cases.expected: Rod can support compression (T < 0), so v_top can be 0, giving u_min = sqrt(4gL) = 2*sqrt(gL)
u_min -> 0, any infinitesimal speed maintains uniform circular motion

independent_check.quick_check: At the bottom, $T_{\text{bottom}} = mg + \frac{m u^2}{L} = mg + 5mg = 6mg$. At the top, $T_{\text{top}} = \frac{m v^2}{L} - mg = mg - mg = 0$. $\Delta T = 6mg$, exactly matching the universal dynamic invariant $\Delta T = 6mg$ for any vertical circular motion on a string.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Angle of slacking $\theta$ from lowest point: In general, $T(\theta) = m \left( \frac{u^2}{L} - 2g + 3g\cos\theta \right)$. For $u = \sqrt{5gL}$: $T(\theta) = mg(5 - 2 + 3\cos\theta) = 3mg(1 + \cos\theta)$. For all $\theta \in [0, \pi]$, $1 + \cos\theta \ge 0$, and at $\theta = \pi$ (top), $T(\pi) = 3mg(1 - 1) = 0$. Tension is strictly positive throughout $[0, \pi)$ and touches zero only at the pinnacle. Fully verified.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT confuse a flexible string with a rigid light rod. A rigid rod can support negative normal force (compression), requiring only $u = \sqrt{4gL}$, whereas a string collapses whenever $T \le 0$, demanding $u = \sqrt{5gL}$.

questions.stem: A uniform flexible rope of total mass $M$ and length $L$ lies completely coiled on a smooth horizontal table. One end is pulled vertically upward at a constant speed $v$. What external upward force $F(y)$ must be applied as a function of the instantaneous height $y$ ($0 \le y \le L$) of the top end?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesizing variable-mass momentum accretion rate dm/dt = lambda*v with Newton's second law F - mg = dp/dt to deduce lifting force F(y) = (M/L)gy + (M/L)v^2.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires formulating momentum transport across an accretion boundary rather than fixed-mass Work-Energy application.

A.diagnostic: Correct: The lifting force must balance both the gravitational weight of the airborne segment W = (M/L)gy and the continuous rate of momentum transfer required to jerk stationary rope segments into upward motion at speed v: v dm/dt = v (lambda v) = (M/L)v^2.

B.diagnostic: Accounts only for the static weight of the lifted section, completely ignoring the dynamic reaction force (momentum flux) caused by accelerating stationary rope links into motion.

C.diagnostic: Confuses the force with the rate of kinetic energy generation dK/dt = 1/2 dm/dt v^2, failing to recognize that inelastic collision impulse dissipates half the input power into internal heat.

D.diagnostic: Treats the entire rope mass M as suspended in the air at all times rather than the instantaneous portion (M/L)y.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What two distinct physical demands must the lifting force satisfy simultaneously as the rope is hoisted at constant speed?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The lifting force must support the instantaneous weight of the hanging portion of the rope AND provide the upward impulse required to accelerate newly lifted segments from rest to speed $v$.

progressive_hints.title: Momentum Flux Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How do you express Newton's Second Law for a variable-mass system moving at constant speed $v$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By the generalized Newton's second law: $F_{\text{ext}} - m(t) g = \frac{dp}{dt} = m\frac{dv}{dt} + v\frac{dm}{dt}$. Since speed is constant ($\frac{dv}{dt} = 0$), $F_{\text{ext}} = m(t) g + v\frac{dm}{dt}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the mass accretion rate $\frac{dm}{dt}$ in terms of linear density $\lambda = M/L$ and speed $v$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Since $m(y) = \lambda y$, $\frac{dm}{dt} = \lambda \frac{dy}{dt} = \lambda v = \frac{M}{L} v$. Substituting: $F(y) = \left(\frac{M}{L} y\right) g + v \left(\frac{M}{L} v\right) = \frac{M}{L} g y + \frac{M}{L} v^2$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: A rope of mass $M$, length $L$ is pulled up from a coil at constant speed $v$. Goal: find lifting force $F(y)$ at height $y$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Linear mass density $\lambda = M / L$. Hanging length: $y$. Hanging mass: $m(y) = \lambda y = (M/L)y$. Upward momentum of hanging rope: $p(t) = m(t) v = \lambda y v$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Apply impulse-momentum theorem over small time $dt$: An element of mass $dm = \lambda dy = \lambda v dt$ at rest on the floor is accelerated to speed $v$. Momentum gained in time $dt$ is $dp = (dm) v = \lambda v^2 dt$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Net external vertical force on the hanging chain: $F_{\text{net}} = F(y) - m(y)g = \frac{dp}{dt} = \lambda v^2$. Therefore, $F(y) = m(y)g + \lambda v^2 = \frac{M}{L} g y + \frac{M}{L} v^2$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The force consists of two distinct physical terms: a linear static weight term $\frac{M}{L}gy$ that increases with height, and an invariant dynamic thrust term $\frac{M}{L}v^2$ that depends quadratically on the lifting speed.

derivation_steps: Define linear mass density: $\lambda = \frac{M}{L}$.
Mass of suspended rope at height $y$: $m(y) = \lambda y$.
Rate of mass entrainment into motion: $\frac{dm}{dt} = \lambda \frac{dy}{dt} = \lambda v$.
Rate of momentum change: $\frac{dp}{dt} = v \frac{dm}{dt} = \lambda v^2 = \frac{M}{L} v^2$.
Newton's Second Law for airborne segment: $F(y) - m(y)g = \frac{dp}{dt}$.
Solve for lifting force: $F(y) = \frac{M}{L} g y + \frac{M}{L} v^2$.

independent_check.quick_check: At completion $y = L$: $F(L) = Mg + \frac{M}{L}v^2$. If $v = 0$, $F(L) = Mg$, matching the static suspended weight of the entire rope.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Energy analysis: Total work done in lifting rope to height $y$ is $W = \int_0^y F(y') dy' = \frac{1}{2}\frac{M}{L}gy^2 + \frac{M}{L}v^2 y$. The mechanical energy stored in the hanging rope is potential energy $U = \left(\frac{M}{L}y\right)g\left(\frac{y}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\frac{M}{L}gy^2$ plus kinetic energy $K = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{M}{L}y\right)v^2 = \frac{1}{2}\frac{M}{L}v^2 y$. Notice $W - (U + K) = \frac{1}{2}\frac{M}{L}v^2 y > 0$. Exactly half of the dynamic work done is dissipated as internal heat through the inelastic jerking of successive rope links from rest. Beautifully consistent with thermodynamics.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT apply naive mechanical energy conservation $W = \Delta E_{\text{mech}}$. The process of jerking stationary mass elements into motion is completely inelastic, dissipating exactly $50\%$ of the dynamic input work.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: WEP-03 (Work-Energy Theorem)

questions.stem: A particle moves in the $xy$-plane subject to a two-dimensional force field $\vec{F}(x,y) = (2xy)\hat{i} + (x^2)\hat{j}$, where force is measured in Newtons and coordinates are in meters. What is the total work done by this force on the particle as it moves from the origin $(0,0)$ to the point $(2,4)\text{ m}$ along any continuous path?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Justifying path independence of 2D force field F = 2xy i + x^2 j by proving curl-free exactness d(x^2 y) and evaluating line integral W = [x^2 y] = 16 J.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires mathematical proof of conservative vector field properties prior to evaluating scalar potential.

A.diagnostic: Correct: The differential work dW = 2xy dx + x^2 dy is an exact differential d(x^2 y) because partial F_y / partial x = 2x = partial F_x / partial y. Hence the work is path-independent: W = [x^2 y]_{(0,0)}^{(2,4)} = (2)^2(4) - 0 = 16 J.

B.diagnostic: Arbitrarily doubles the result or evaluates F_x Delta x + F_y Delta y at maximum coordinates (2*2*4*2 + 2^2 * 4 = 32 + 16).

C.diagnostic: Evaluates work along the parabolic path y = x^2 with an erroneous factor of 1/2.

D.diagnostic: Averages initial and final force magnitudes naively along the straight line without performing the exact line integral.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How can you test whether a 2D force field $\vec{F} = F_x\hat{i} + F_y\hat{j}$ is conservative and path-independent?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: A 2D force field is conservative if and only if its curl vanishes: $\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y}$. Test this: $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2) = 2x$, and $\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(2xy) = 2x$. They are identical!

progressive_hints.title: Exact Differential Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the differential work $dW = \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = F_x dx + F_y dy$, and can it be written as the total differential of a single function?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $dW = 2xy dx + x^2 dy$. Notice by the product rule that $d(x^2 y) = (d(x^2)) y + x^2 (dy) = (2x dx) y + x^2 dy = 2xy dx + x^2 dy$. Thus $dW = d(x^2 y)$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How do you evaluate the path-independent work integral between $(0,0)$ and $(2,4)$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Integrate the exact differential directly: $W = \int_{(0,0)}^{(2,4)} d(x^2 y) = \left[ x^2 y \right]_{(0,0)}^{(2,4)} = (2)^2 (4) - (0)^2 (0) = 4 \times 4 = 16\text{ J}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Particle moves from $(0,0)$ to $(2,4)$ in force field $\vec{F} = (2xy)\hat{i} + (x^2)\hat{j}$. Goal: find work done along any continuous path.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Differential displacement: $d\vec{r} = dx\hat{i} + dy\hat{j}$. Work element: $dW = \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = 2xy dx + x^2 dy$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Check condition for conservative force: $\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2) = 2x$, and $\frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(2xy) = 2x$. Because $\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y}$, the field is conservative, meaning $dW$ is an exact differential.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Identify scalar potential: $\vec{F} = -\nabla U \implies -dU = dW = d(x^2 y) \implies U(x,y) = -x^2 y + C$. Work done: $W = -\Delta U = -[U(2,4) - U(0,0)] = [x^2 y]_{(0,0)}^{(2,4)} = (2^2)(4) - (0^2)(0) = 16\text{ J}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Because the work done depends purely on the coordinates of the endpoints and is strictly zero around any closed contour ($\oint \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = 0$), the force field is conservative with work equal to $16\text{ J}$ along every conceivable path.

derivation_steps: Identify force components: $F_x = 2xy$ and $F_y = x^2$.
Test exactness: $\frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y} = 2x = \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x}$. Condition satisfied (curl-free).
Express differential work: $dW = 2xy dx + x^2 dy = d(x^2 y)$.
Set up definite integral: $W = \int_{(0,0)}^{(2,4)} d(x^2 y)$.
Evaluate at boundary points: $W = (2)^2 \times 4 - (0)^2 \times 0 = 4 \times 4 = 16\text{ J}$.

limiting_cases.expected: W = oint F . dr = 0 J (path independence property)

limiting_cases.condition: Target point at (0, 4) along y-axis where x=0
limiting_cases.expected: W = 0 J since F_x = 0 and F_y = 0 along entire y-axis

independent_check.quick_check: Straight-line path $y = 2x$: Then $dy = 2 dx$, and $dW = 2x(2x) dx + x^2 (2 dx) = 4x^2 dx + 2x^2 dx = 6x^2 dx$. Integrating from $x=0$ to $x=2$: $W = \int_0^2 6x^2 dx = [2x^3]_0^2 = 2(8) = 16\text{ J}$. Exactly identical.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Two-step rectangular path: Path 1: $(0,0) \to (2,0)$ along x-axis ($y=0, dy=0$). Here $F_x = 2x(0) = 0$, so $W_1 = 0$. Path 2: $(2,0) \to (2,4)$ parallel to y-axis ($x=2, dx=0$). Here $F_y = x^2 = 4$, so $W_2 = \int_0^4 4 dy = 4 \times 4 = 16\text{ J}$. Total work $W = W_1 + W_2 = 0 + 16 = 16\text{ J}$. Conclusively verified across three independent trajectories.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT assume a force is non-conservative just because it depends on both coordinates ($x$ and $y$). Always verify the curl condition $\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y} = 0$.

questions.stem: An electric dragster of mass $m$ starts from rest at $t = 0$ along a straight horizontal frictionless track, driven by a high-performance motor that delivers a constant mechanical power output $P$. Neglecting all aerodynamic drag and rotational inertia of the wheels, what is the position $s(t)$ of the vehicle as a function of elapsed time $t$?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesizing constant power energy accumulation W = Pt = 1/2 m v^2 with differential velocity integration s = int v dt to establish s(t) = sqrt(8P/9m) t^(3/2).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires quadrature over a time-dependent non-uniform acceleration field rather than algebraic kinematics.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Work W = Pt = 1/2 m v^2 yields v(t) = sqrt(2P/m) t^(1/2). Integrating s(t) = int_0^t v dt = sqrt(2P/m) (2/3 t^(3/2)) = sqrt(8P/9m) t^(3/2).

B.diagnostic: Omits the integration factor 2/3 resulting from int t^(1/2) dt, naively multiplying velocity v(t) by time t.

C.diagnostic: Mistakenly assumes constant acceleration a = P/m and applies the standard constant-acceleration formula s = 1/2 a t^2, ignoring that acceleration decreases as velocity increases (a = P/(mv)).

D.diagnostic: Dimensionally invalid expression that assumes a linear relationship between position and time.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the relationship between constant power $P$, elapsed time $t$, and the kinetic energy of a body starting from rest?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Because power is constant, total work done in time $t$ is $W = P \times t$. By the Work-Energy Theorem, this equals the vehicle's kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = P t$.

progressive_hints.title: Velocity Kinematic Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How does the velocity of the vehicle scale with time $t$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Solving for velocity: $v(t) = \sqrt{\frac{2 P t}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 P}{m}} \, t^{1/2}$. Notice velocity is proportional to $\sqrt{t}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How do you obtain position $s(t)$ by integrating $v(t) = \frac{ds}{dt}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Integrate $v(t)$ with respect to time: $s(t) = \int_0^t \sqrt{\frac{2 P}{m}} t'^{1/2} dt' = \sqrt{\frac{2 P}{m}} \left[ \frac{2}{3} t^{3/2} \right]$. Bringing $\frac{2}{3}$ into the square root gives $\sqrt{\frac{4 \times 2 P}{9 m}} t^{3/2} = \sqrt{\frac{8 P}{9 m}} t^{3/2}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Dragster mass $m$ starts from rest, accelerated by constant engine power $P$. Track is frictionless. Goal: find position $s(t)$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Power definition: $P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = m v \frac{dv}{dt}$. Starting conditions: $v(0) = 0$, $s(0) = 0$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Work-Energy Theorem: Total work done from $0$ to $t$ is $W(t) = \int_0^t P dt' = P t$. Equating to kinetic energy: $W(t) = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 - 0$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Speed: $v(t) = \sqrt{\frac{2 P}{m}} t^{1/2}$. Distance traveled: $s(t) = \int_0^t v(t') dt' = \sqrt{\frac{2 P}{m}} \int_0^t t'^{1/2} dt' = \sqrt{\frac{2 P}{m}} \left( \frac{2}{3} t^{3/2} \right) = \sqrt{\frac{8 P}{9 m}} t^{3/2}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Unlike constant acceleration where $s \propto t^2$, under constant power the force $F = P/v$ decreases as speed increases, leading to a sub-quadratic scaling $s \propto t^{3/2}$.

derivation_steps: Work done by constant power: $W = \int_0^t P dt' = P t$.
Apply Work-Energy Theorem: $\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = P t$.
Express instantaneous velocity: $v(t) = \left( \frac{2 P}{m} \right)^{1/2} t^{1/2}$.
Integrate to find position: $s(t) = \int_0^t v(t') dt' = \left( \frac{2 P}{m} \right)^{1/2} \left[ \frac{2}{3} t'^{3/2} \right]_0^t$.
Simplify algebraic coefficient: $\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{\frac{2 P}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{8 P}{9 m}}$, so $s(t) = \sqrt{\frac{8 P}{9 m}} t^{3/2}$.

independent_check.quick_check: Differentiate $s(t)$ twice to check power $P = m v a$: Velocity $v(t) = s'(t) = \sqrt{\frac{8P}{9m}} \cdot \frac{3}{2} t^{1/2} = \sqrt{\frac{2P}{m}} t^{1/2}$. Acceleration $a(t) = v'(t) = \sqrt{\frac{2P}{m}} \cdot \frac{1}{2} t^{-1/2} = \sqrt{\frac{P}{2m}} t^{-1/2}$. Power: $P(t) = m v(t) a(t) = m \left(\sqrt{\frac{2P}{m}} t^{1/2}\right) \left(\sqrt{\frac{P}{2m}} t^{-1/2}\right) = m \sqrt{\frac{P^2}{m^2}} = P$. Matches perfectly and identically for all $t > 0$!
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Alternative derivation via $F = m v \frac{dv}{ds}$: Since $P = F v = m v^2 \frac{dv}{ds}$, we separate variables: $m v^2 dv = P ds$. Integrating from $0$ to $v$ and $0$ to $s$: $\frac{1}{3} m v^3 = P s \implies s = \frac{m v^3}{3 P}$. Substitute $v = (2Pt/m)^{1/2}$: $v^3 = (2Pt/m)^{3/2}$. Thus $s = \frac{m}{3P} \left(\frac{2Pt}{m}\right)^{3/2} = \frac{m}{3P} \frac{2\sqrt{2} P^{3/2} t^{3/2}}{m^{3/2}} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \sqrt{\frac{P}{m}} t^{3/2} = \sqrt{\frac{8P}{9m}} t^{3/2}$. Two completely different differential equations yield identical results.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT confuse constant power with constant force! A vehicle with constant power has an infinite acceleration at $t=0$ that continuously drops as $t^{-1/2}$, whereas constant force yields uniform acceleration and $s \propto t^2$.

questions.stem: A particle of mass $m$ moves in a one-dimensional potential energy well given by $U(x) = \frac{a}{x^2} - \frac{b}{x}$ for $x > 0$, where $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ are positive physical constants representing short-range repulsion and long-range attraction, respectively. What is the binding energy $E_b$ of the particle in this potential well (the minimum energy required to liberate the particle from its stable equilibrium position to infinity where $U(\infty) = 0$)?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling molecular potential well U(x) = a/x^2 - b/x by determining stationary point F = -dU/dx = 0 at x_0 = 2a/b and computing bound-state ionization threshold E_b = 0 - U(x_0) = b^2/(4a).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires extremum differential calculus and stability analysis on an asymmetric potential landscape.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Equilibrium occurs where F = -dU/dx = 0 => -2a/x^3 + b/x^2 = 0 => x_0 = 2a/b. Substituting into potential: U(x_0) = a/(4a^2/b^2) - b/(2a/b) = b^2/(4a) - b^2/(2a) = -b^2/(4a). The binding energy is E_b = U(infinity) - U(x_0) = 0 - (-b^2/(4a)) = b^2/(4a).

B.diagnostic: Omits the coefficient 2 in the derivative of x^(-2), getting erroneous equilibrium position x_0 = a/b and depth -b^2/(2a).

C.diagnostic: Neglects the repulsive term's contribution at equilibrium, evaluating simply -b/x_0 with an arbitrary scale.

D.diagnostic: Dimensionally inverted expression ([a/b^2] = [J]^(-1)), confusing numerator and denominator.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the physical condition for finding the equilibrium position $x_0$ in any conservative potential field $U(x)$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Equilibrium occurs where the conservative force vanishes: $F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$. For a stable bound state, this must be a local minimum ($\frac{d^2 U}{dx^2} > 0$).

progressive_hints.title: Equilibrium Position Calculation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the derivative $\frac{dU}{dx}$ of $U(x) = a x^{-2} - b x^{-1}$, and what is its root $x_0$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\frac{dU}{dx} = -2a x^{-3} + b x^{-2} = \frac{-2a + bx}{x^3}$. Setting this to zero gives $-2a + bx_0 = 0 \implies x_0 = \frac{2a}{b}$. Because $\frac{d^2 U}{dx^2} > 0$ at $x_0$, this is a stable minimum.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the potential depth $U(x_0)$ at the bottom of the well, and how is binding energy defined?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Substitute $x_0 = \frac{2a}{b}$: $U(x_0) = \frac{a}{(2a/b)^2} - \frac{b}{(2a/b)} = \frac{b^2}{4a} - \frac{b^2}{2a} = -\frac{b^2}{4a}$. Binding energy is the energy needed to escape to infinity: $E_b = U(\infty) - U(x_0) = 0 - \left(-\frac{b^2}{4a}\right) = \frac{b^2}{4a}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Potential well $U(x) = \frac{a}{x^2} - \frac{b}{x}$ for $x > 0$ with $a,b > 0$. Goal: find binding energy $E_b = U(\infty) - U_{\text{min}}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Force is negative gradient of potential: $F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx}$. Asymptote at infinity: $\lim_{x \to \infty} U(x) = 0$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Stable equilibrium requires $F(x_0) = 0$ with $\frac{d^2 U}{dx^2}(x_0) > 0$. Binding energy is the depth of the well: $E_b = 0 - U(x_0)$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: 1. Derivative: $\frac{dU}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx}(a x^{-2} - b x^{-1}) = -2a x^{-3} + b x^{-2}$. 2. Solve $-2a/x^3 + b/x^2 = 0 \implies x_0 = 2a/b$. 3. Curvature: $\frac{d^2 U}{dx^2} = 6a x^{-4} - 2b x^{-3} = \frac{6a - 2b(2a/b)}{(2a/b)^4} = \frac{2a}{(2a/b)^4} > 0$ (stable). 4. Value: $U(x_0) = \frac{a}{(2a/b)^2} - \frac{b}{(2a/b)} = \frac{a b^2}{4 a^2} - \frac{b^2}{2a} = \frac{b^2}{4a} - \frac{2b^2}{4a} = -\frac{b^2}{4a}$. 5. Binding energy: $E_b = -U(x_0) = \frac{b^2}{4a}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The particle is trapped in an attractive potential well with depth $\frac{b^2}{4a}$. To reach infinity at rest, an external agent must supply at least $E_b = \frac{b^2}{4a}$ of work.

derivation_steps: Formulate force: $F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx} = -\left( -\frac{2a}{x^3} + \frac{b}{x^2} \right) = \frac{2a - bx}{x^3}$.
Find equilibrium point: $F(x_0) = 0 \implies 2a - bx_0 = 0 \implies x_0 = \frac{2a}{b}$.
Verify stability: $\frac{d^2 U}{dx^2}\Big|_{x_0} = \frac{2a}{x_0^4} > 0$, confirming a potential well minimum.
Evaluate minimum potential: $U_{\text{min}} = U(x_0) = \frac{a}{(2a/b)^2} - \frac{b}{(2a/b)} = \frac{b^2}{4a} - \frac{b^2}{2a} = -\frac{b^2}{4a}$.
Calculate binding energy: $E_b = U(\infty) - U_{\text{min}} = 0 - \left( -\frac{b^2}{4a} \right) = \frac{b^2}{4a}$.

limiting_cases.condition: a -> infinity (Infinite repulsive core at large distance)
limiting_cases.expected: E_b -> 0 (Well is pushed out and flattened)

independent_check.quick_check: Completing the square in $1/x$: Let $u = 1/x$. Then $U(u) = a u^2 - b u = a \left(u - \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 - \frac{b^2}{4a}$. Because $a > 0$, the quadratic in $u$ has its absolute minimum when $u = \frac{b}{2a}$ (so $x = \frac{2a}{b}$), and the minimum value is identically $-\frac{b^2}{4a}$! This bypasses calculus entirely and proves algebraically that $E_b = \frac{b^2}{4a}$.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Small oscillation frequency $\omega_0$ in the well: Near $x_0$, $U(x) \approx U(x_0) + \frac{1}{2} k_{\text{eff}} (x - x_0)^2$ where $k_{\text{eff}} = \frac{2a}{x_0^4} = \frac{2a}{(16 a^4 / b^4)} = \frac{b^4}{8 a^3}$. Depth estimate: $\Delta U \approx k_{\text{eff}} x_0^2 = \frac{b^4}{8 a^3} \frac{4 a^2}{b^2} = \frac{b^2}{2a}$, on the exact order of magnitude of $E_b = \frac{b^2}{4a}$.
independent_check.watch_out: Binding energy is defined as a positive quantity $E_b = U(\infty) - U(x_0) > 0$. Do NOT return the negative well depth $-b^2/(4a)$.
